title: GPS + IMU Sensor Fusion
text:
← Back to Gallery
Topic: Kalman filtering — fusing GPS with a phone gyroscope so the track keeps going through a tunnel, where GPS drops out and dead reckoning takes over. Chapter: 6 — Processing of the Signal



The one thing GPS cannot do is work indoors, in tunnels, or under an overpass: with too few satellites in view, the fix simply stops. A car’s navigation display keeps moving anyway — because it dead-reckons through the gap using inertial sensors. This example reproduces that from a real drive: we take a clean GPS track, artificially blank a 12-second segment to simulate a tunnel, and let a Kalman filter coast through it on the phone’s gyroscope.
Two sensors, two complementary weaknesses. GPS gives an absolute position — here the phone’s GNSS-chip fix, which is a pure satellite solution (Android’s GPS provider, not the sensor-blended fused provider, so it carries no IMU information of its own). It is accurate to a few metres but vanishes without a sky view. The gyroscope is quiet, fast (100 Hz), and never loses signal, but it measures only a turn rate: integrate it and the heading drifts without bound. The Kalman filter leans on GPS whenever it is available and on the gyro whenever it is not.
The data is a real 3.4 km drive through the Berkeley hills, logged with Google’s GnssLogger: 1 Hz GPS fixes and a 100 Hz gyroscope, phone lying flat on the dash.



The state is position and velocity in a local east–north (ENU) frame, \mathbf{x} = [\,E\; N\; v_E\; v_N\,]^\mathsf{T}.
Predict. A constant-velocity model advances position by \mathbf{v}\,\Delta t, but the velocity direction is rotated by the heading change \Delta\psi from the gyroscope — so through a bend the prediction turns with the car instead of flying off straight. That rotation is the whole reason dead reckoning survives a curve:

F_k = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & \Delta t & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & \Delta t \\ 0 & 0 & \cos\Delta\psi_k & \sin\Delta\psi_k \\ 0 & 0 & -\sin\Delta\psi_k & \cos\Delta\psi_k \end{bmatrix},
\qquad \Delta\psi_k = \int_{t_{k-1}}^{t_k}\!\dot\psi\,dt .

Only the change in heading is used, so the arbitrary yaw origin cancels; the gyro’s scale and bias are calibrated once against the GPS course-over-ground (the phone lay flat, so its vertical-axis rate ≈ the vehicle’s turn rate, a correlation of −0.95).
Update. Each GPS fix corrects the position through the standard Kalman gain, gated by a normalised-innovation (NIS) \chi^2 test against multipath. Inside the tunnel every fix is withheld and the state coasts on the prediction alone. On the way out, the estimate is stale, so the covariance is inflated — otherwise the gate would reject the perfectly good re-acquired fix as an “outlier” and the filter would never recover.



import numpy as np

d = np.load('Data/kalman_gps_imu.npz')
gt, E, N, gacc = d['gt'], d['E'], d['N'], d['gacc']     # GPS fixes: time, east, north, accuracy
gz_t, gz   = d['gz_time'], d['gz']                      # gyro: time, vertical-axis rate
slope, icpt = float(d['slope']), float(d['icpt'])       # gyro→heading-rate calibration
OUT = tuple(d['outage'])                                # (t0, t1) of the simulated tunnel

# heading change per step: integrate the gyro on a fine grid (coarse sampling aliases turns)
dt = 0.25;  T = np.arange(0, gt[-1] + dt, dt)
fdt = 0.01; FT = np.arange(0, gt[-1] + dt, fdt)
psi = np.concatenate(([0], np.cumsum((slope*np.interp(FT, gz_t, gz) + icpt)[:-1]) * fdt))
dyaw = np.diff(np.interp(T, FT, psi), prepend=0.0)

def kalman(qa=3.0, outage=None, coast_in_outage=False):
    x = np.array([E[0], N[0], 0., 0.]);  P = np.diag([25., 25, 4, 4])
    gi = 0; track = []; was_in = False
    for k, tk in enumerate(T):
        in_tunnel = outage and outage[0] <= tk <= outage[1]
        if was_in and not in_tunnel:                    # re-acquiring GPS after the blackout:
            P = np.diag([1e4, 1e4, 1e2, 1e2])           # inflate covariance so the gate trusts it
        was_in = in_tunnel
        c, s = np.cos(dyaw[k]), np.sin(dyaw[k])
        R = np.eye(2) if (coast_in_outage and in_tunnel) else np.array([[c, s], [-s, c]])
        Fm = np.eye(4); Fm[0, 2] = Fm[1, 3] = dt; Fm[2:, 2:] = R   # rotate velocity by Δψ
        G = np.array([[dt*dt/2, 0], [0, dt*dt/2], [dt, 0], [0, dt]])
        x = Fm @ x;  P = Fm @ P @ Fm.T + G @ np.diag([qa**2, qa**2]) @ G.T   # predict
        while gi < len(gt) and gt[gi] <= tk + dt/2:                          # fold in GPS fixes
            if gt[gi] > tk - dt/2:
                blocked = outage and outage[0] <= gt[gi] <= outage[1]        # inside the tunnel
                H = np.array([[1, 0, 0, 0], [0, 1., 0, 0]]); Rm = np.diag([max(gacc[gi], 5.)**2]*2)
                y = np.array([E[gi], N[gi]]) - H @ x
                S = H @ P @ H.T + Rm
                if not (blocked or y @ np.linalg.solve(S, y) > 13.8):        # NIS χ² gate
                    K = P @ H.T @ np.linalg.inv(S)
                    x = x + K @ y;  P = (np.eye(4) - K @ H) @ P
            gi += 1
        track.append(x.copy())
    return np.array(track)

fused = kalman()                                        # GPS present the whole time
gyro  = kalman(outage=OUT)                              # keep gyro-steering through the tunnel
coast = kalman(outage=OUT, coast_in_outage=True)        # freeze heading in the tunnel (no IMU)







Dead reckoning through a simulated tunnel on a 3.4 km Berkeley-hills drive. (a) The Kalman-fused track (blue) over the 1 Hz GPS chip fixes (grey); the red segment near the start is the 12 s stretch where GPS was blanked. (b) Inside the tunnel — a sharp hairpin: keeping the gyroscope, the filter dead-reckons around the corner and stays on the road (blue); without it, freezing the heading, the track coasts straight off the hillside (red). The grey dots are the hidden true GPS. (c) Position error vs time: the no-IMU coast climbs to ~60 m before GPS returns and snaps it back, while the gyro holds ~10 m throughout.



The story is in panel (b). Both filters are identical up to the tunnel mouth; inside, one keeps rotating its velocity with the gyroscope and the other holds its last heading. Over a 12-second hairpin that difference is decisive: the gyro-steered estimate rounds the corner and comes out ≈ 11 m from the truth, while the heading-frozen coast drives straight and exits ≈ 60 m away — well off the road. Panel (c) shows the same thing in time: the coast error grows without bound until GPS returns and yanks it back, whereas the gyro keeps the error flat.
A few honest notes. The gyroscope buys time, not permanent accuracy — the error in (c) is still creeping upward, just slowly; dead reckoning is a loan repaid when GPS returns, good for the tens of seconds it takes to clear a tunnel, not for minutes. The outage is simulated by hiding otherwise-good fixes, which is what lets us score the dead-reckoning against the known truth. The gyro was calibrated once against the GPS course (a scale-and-bias fit, not a magnetometer heading), and the covariance inflation on re-acquisition is the small piece of book-keeping that lets the filter accept GPS again after coasting blind.

See Chapter 6 for filtering fundamentals. Map tiles © OpenStreetMap contributors, © CARTO. The processed drive is shipped as Data/kalman_gps_imu.npz.

title: Piano String Inharmonicity
text:
← Back to Gallery
Topic: Spectral peak detection and nonlinear curve fitting — measuring piano string stiffness from a recording. Chapter: 2 — Frequency Domain



An ideal string produces overtones at exact integer multiples n f_1 of the fundamental. A real piano string is a stiff beam: bending stiffness stretches every partial slightly sharp according to the Euler–Bernoulli inharmonicity formula. Spectral analysis makes this deviation directly measurable.



Solving the stiff-string wave equation

\mu \frac{\partial^2 y}{\partial t^2} = T\frac{\partial^2 y}{\partial x^2} - EI\frac{\partial^4 y}{\partial x^4}

with fixed-end boundary conditions gives the partial frequencies

f_n = n f_1 \sqrt{1 + B n^2}, \qquad B = \frac{\pi^2 E I}{T L^2}

The inharmonicity coefficient B is fitted from the positions of the spectral peaks. For a concert grand at middle C, B \sim 2\times10^{-4} — small per note but large enough that piano tuners must apply octave stretch to keep the instrument in tune across the keyboard.



import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import matplotlib.ticker as ticker
import scienceplots
from scipy.signal import welch, find_peaks
from scipy.optimize import curve_fit

plt.style.use(['science', 'nature', 'notebook', 'grid', 'high-vis'])

# ── Synthesise middle-C piano note (16 inharmonic partials) ──────────────
f1 = 261.63          # fundamental – middle C [Hz]
B  = 2.6e-4          # inharmonicity coefficient (concert grand, C4)
fs = 44_100          # sample rate [Hz]
N  = int(fs * 2.0)   # 2-second note
t  = np.arange(N) / fs

sig = np.zeros(N)
for n in range(1, 17):
    fn   = n * f1 * np.sqrt(1 + B * n**2)
    sig += (1.0 / n**0.65) * np.sin(2 * np.pi * fn * t) * np.exp(-t / (0.6 + 3.0 / n))
sig += 0.008 * np.random.default_rng(42).standard_normal(N)

# ── Welch PSD ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
freq, psd = welch(sig, fs=fs, nperseg=N // 4, window='hann')

# ── Harmonic peak detection ───────────────────────────────────────────────
peak_idx, _ = find_peaks(np.log10(psd + 1e-20), prominence=0.3,
                          distance=int(f1 * 0.7 / (freq[1] - freq[0])))
peak_idx = peak_idx[freq[peak_idx] < 5000]
n_det    = peak_idx.size
n_nums   = np.arange(1, n_det + 1)

# ── Fit inharmonicity model ───────────────────────────────────────────────
popt, _ = curve_fit(lambda n, B: f1 * n * np.sqrt(1 + B * n * n),
                    n_nums, freq[peak_idx], p0=[1e-4])
B_fit = popt[0]

# ── Plot ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
plt.close()
plt.figure(figsize=(8, 4))
ax1 = plt.subplot(1, 2, 1)
ax2 = plt.subplot(1, 2, 2)

ax1.semilogy(freq, psd, 'k-', lw=0.8)
ax1.semilogy(freq[peak_idx], psd[peak_idx], 'C0o', ms=4)
ax1.set_xlim(0, 5000)
ax1.set_xlabel('Frequency [Hz]')
ax1.set_ylabel('Power Spectral Density [Arb$^2$/Hz]')

n_dense = np.linspace(0.8, n_det + 0.3, 300)
ax2.plot(n_nums, freq[peak_idx], 'C0o', ms=4, label='Measured peaks')
ax2.plot(n_dense, f1 * n_dense, 'k--', alpha=0.6, label='$nf_1$  (ideal)')
ax2.plot(n_dense, f1 * n_dense * np.sqrt(1 + B_fit * n_dense**2),
         'C1-', lw=1.5, label=fr'Fit  $B={B_fit:.2e}$')
ax2.xaxis.set_major_locator(ticker.MultipleLocator(2))
ax2.set_xlabel('Harmonic Number')
ax2.set_ylabel('Frequency [Hz]')
ax2.legend(loc='upper left', ncol=1, labelcolor=['C0', 'k', 'C1'], frameon=False)

plt.suptitle('Piano String Inharmonicity', fontsize=16, weight='bold', style='italic')
plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig('figure_piano_harmonic.png', bbox_inches='tight', dpi=300)







Piano C4 power spectrum (left) and inharmonic overtone positions fitted with the stiff-string model (right)



Panel (a) shows the Welch PSD of a synthesised middle-C piano note; red dots mark the 16 detected partials. Panel (b) plots their frequencies against harmonic number: the dashed line is the ideal harmonic series n f_1, the orange curve is the fitted stiff-string model n f_1\sqrt{1+Bn^2} with B \approx 2 \times 10^{-4}. The upward curvature grows rapidly above n \approx 10, which is why the highest bass strings of a concert grand deviate by more than a semitone from equal temperament at the upper partials.

See Chapter 2 for the Euler–Bernoulli derivation and the connection between octave stretch and inharmonicity.

title: Aliasing & the Nyquist Folding Receiver
text:
← Back to Gallery
Topic: The Nyquist–Shannon sampling theorem — and how a modulated sample clock turns aliasing from a hazard into a wideband-receiver architecture. Chapter: 1 — Data Initialization



Sampling converts a continuous signal into a discrete sequence. The Nyquist theorem says perfect reconstruction is possible only if the sampling rate exceeds twice the highest frequency, f_s > 2f_\text{max}. Violate it and high frequencies fold back to lower ones — aliasing. A sinusoid at f_0 sampled at f_s is indistinguishable from one at

f_\text{alias} = \left| \left( f_0 + \tfrac{f_s}{2} \right) \bmod f_s - \tfrac{f_s}{2} \right|.

For f_0 = 1.2 kHz and f_s = 1 kHz the spectrum reports 200 Hz, though the signal was at 1.2 kHz:




A 1.2 kHz tone sampled at 1 kHz appears at 200 Hz; at 3 kHz it is correct



But the deeper problem is ambiguity — any Nyquist zone folds to the same place. Sample at 20 Hz, and a 3 Hz tone and a 17 Hz tone produce literally identical samples; so do 6 Hz and 26 Hz:




Four different tones — 3, 17, 6, and 26 Hz — sampled at 20 Hz. Each column yields exactly the same red sample sequence: from the samples alone, the zones are indistinguishable.



Undersample a wide band and you cannot tell where a signal really was. Usually we forbid this with an anti-aliasing filter. The Nyquist Folding Receiver (NYFR) does the opposite — it embraces the folding and adds one trick to undo the ambiguity.



A wideband receiver wants to watch many GHz but can only afford a slow ADC. The NYFR deliberately undersamples the whole band so every Nyquist zone folds down onto the first — and drives the sample-and-hold with a phase-modulated clock instead of a uniform one. If the sampling instants carry a small sinusoidal jitter \delta t(k) = A_j \sin(2\pi f_m k / f_s), a tone at RF frequency f_\text{RF} picks up an induced phase

\phi(k) = 2\pi f_\text{RF}\,\delta t(k) = \underbrace{2\pi f_\text{RF} A_j}_{\text{FM index}}\,\sin\!\left(2\pi \tfrac{f_m}{f_s} k\right).

The tone still lands at its baseband alias, but now wearing an induced FM whose depth is proportional to f_\text{RF} — i.e. to the Nyquist zone. Read the FM depth off a spectrogram and you recover which zone the signal came from, and hence its true frequency. One slow ADC, the whole band, ambiguity resolved.



import numpy as np
from scipy import signal

fs = 1.0                                   # normalised sample rate (freqs in units of fs)
N, k = 6000, np.arange(6000)
fm, Aj = 0.0005, 8.0                       # clock-modulation frequency and jitter amplitude

# three tones in Nyquist zones 1, 3, 5 — all fold to distinct baseband aliases
tones = [(0.10, 1), (1.25, 3), (2.40, 5)]  # (f_RF in units of fs, zone)

t_uniform = k / fs                                     # ordinary clock  -> plain aliasing
t_nyfr    = k / fs + Aj*np.sin(2*np.pi*fm*k/fs)        # modulated clock -> zone tagging
mix = lambda t: sum(np.cos(2*np.pi*f*t) for f, _ in tones)

f, tt, S = signal.spectrogram(mix(t_nyfr), fs=fs, nperseg=128, noverlap=120, window='hann')
# in S, each tone sits at its alias with a sinusoidal FM of depth 2*pi*f_RF*Aj*fm  ∝  zone







Nyquist Folding Receiver. (a) With a uniform clock, three tones from Nyquist zones 1, 3, 5 fold to flat baseband lines — you cannot tell which zone each came from. (b) With the modulated clock, the same three lines acquire a sinusoidal FM whose depth grows with the true RF frequency: zone 1 stays flat, zone 3 wiggles moderately, zone 5 swings widely — so the zone, and the real frequency, are recovered.



Both panels show the same three tones landing at baseband aliases 0.10, 0.25, 0.40 f_s. Under a uniform clock (a) they are flat lines — a 0.40 f_s line could be a zone-1 tone at 0.40 f_s, a zone-3 tone at 1.60 f_s, a zone-5 tone at 2.40 f_s, and so on; nothing distinguishes them. The modulated clock (b) breaks the tie: because the induced FM depth is \propto f_\text{RF}, the zone-5 tone swings roughly 24× wider than the zone-1 tone. Measuring that swing recovers the Nyquist zone and reconstructs the true RF frequency — the principle behind analog-to-information receivers that cover many GHz of spectrum with a single modest ADC.
The lesson cuts both ways: aliasing is a hazard you normally filter out before sampling — but understood precisely, the same folding can be engineered into a feature.

See Chapter 1 for the sampling theorem, reconstruction, the anti-aliasing filter, and the Nyquist Folding Receiver.

title: Aliasing & the Nyquist Folding Receiver
text:
Sampling converts a continuous signal into a discrete sequence. The Nyquist theorem says perfect reconstruction is possible only if the sampling rate exceeds twice the highest frequency, f_s > 2f_\text{max}. Violate it and high frequencies fold back to lower ones — aliasing. A sinusoid at f_0 sampled at f_s is indistinguishable from one at

f_\text{alias} = \left| \left( f_0 + \tfrac{f_s}{2} \right) \bmod f_s - \tfrac{f_s}{2} \right|.

For f_0 = 1.2 kHz and f_s = 1 kHz the spectrum reports 200 Hz, though the signal was at 1.2 kHz:




A 1.2 kHz tone sampled at 1 kHz appears at 200 Hz; at 3 kHz it is correct



But the deeper problem is ambiguity — any Nyquist zone folds to the same place. Sample at 20 Hz, and a 3 Hz tone and a 17 Hz tone produce literally identical samples; so do 6 Hz and 26 Hz:




Four different tones — 3, 17, 6, and 26 Hz — sampled at 20 Hz. Each column yields exactly the same red sample sequence: from the samples alone, the zones are indistinguishable.



Undersample a wide band and you cannot tell where a signal really was. Usually we forbid this with an anti-aliasing filter. The Nyquist Folding Receiver (NYFR) does the opposite — it embraces the folding and adds one trick to undo the ambiguity.

title: Aliasing
text:
A sinusoid at frequency f_0 sampled at rate f_s is indistinguishable from a sinusoid at the aliased frequency

f_\text{alias} = \left| \left( f_0 + \frac{f_s}{2} \right) \bmod f_s - \frac{f_s}{2} \right|

For f_0 = 1.2 kHz and f_s = 1 kHz: f_\text{alias} = |1.2 - 1.0| = 0.2 kHz. The spectrum reports a 200 Hz tone, though the physical signal was at 1.2 kHz.

title: Spectral Leakage & Windowing
text:
← Back to Gallery
Topic: Window functions — controlling the trade-off between frequency resolution and spectral leakage. Chapter: 4 — More about FFT



When a finite-length DFT is applied to a sinusoid whose frequency does not fall exactly on a DFT bin, the spectral energy leaks into all other bins. This spectral leakage can hide weak tones near strong ones. Multiplying the time-domain signal by a window function that tapers smoothly to zero at the edges suppresses the sidelobe levels, at the cost of widening the main lobe (reduced resolution). Different windows offer different points on this trade-off curve.



Windowing is equivalent to convolving the true spectrum with the window’s own spectrum (the DTFT of the window):

\hat{X}_w(f) = \hat{X}(f) * W(f), \quad W(f) = \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} w[n]\, e^{-j2\pi fn/N}

Key window metrics:









Window
Main-lobe width
Peak sidelobe
Use case




Rectangular
2/N
−13 dB
Transients, well-separated tones


Hann
4/N
−31 dB
General purpose


Blackman
6/N
−57 dB
Weak tones near strong ones


Kaiser (\beta=8)
\sim 5/N
−80 dB
Adjustable sidelobe control






import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

N = 1024
fs = 1.0
f_tone = 0.21 + 0.5 / N   # deliberately off-grid

t = np.arange(N)
x = np.cos(2 * np.pi * f_tone * t)

windows = {
    'Rectangular': np.ones(N),
    'Hann':        np.hanning(N),
    'Blackman':    np.blackman(N),
    'Kaiser β=8':  np.kaiser(N, beta=8),
}

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 5))

for name, w in windows.items():
    X = np.fft.rfft(x * w, n=N * 8)   # zero-pad for interpolation
    freqs = np.fft.rfftfreq(N * 8, d=1.0 / fs)
    power_dB = 20 * np.log10(np.abs(X) / N + 1e-15)
    ax.plot(freqs, power_dB, lw=0.9, label=name)

ax.set_xlim(0, 0.5)
ax.set_ylim(-120, 5)
ax.set_xlabel('Normalised frequency (cycles/sample)')
ax.set_ylabel('Power (dB)')
ax.legend()
plt.tight_layout()







Spectral leakage comparison: rectangular, Hann, Blackman, and Kaiser windows



The rectangular window keeps the main lobe narrow but sidelobes reach only −13 dB. The Blackman window suppresses sidelobes to below −57 dB, making it possible to detect a tone 1000× weaker sitting just a few bins away from a strong one.

See Chapter 4 for zero-padding, window design criteria, and the scalloping-loss correction.

title: Gear-Box Fault Detection
text:
← Back to Gallery
Topic: Cepstrum analysis — separating source and transmission-path contributions in machinery vibration. Chapter: 2 — Frequency Domain



A rotating gear-box produces vibration at the gear-mesh frequency f_\text{mesh} = N_\text{teeth} \times f_\text{shaft} and its harmonics. A bearing fault modulates these harmonics at the fault frequency f_\text{fault}, creating a comb-like family of sidebands in the power spectrum. The cepstrum lifts the log-spectrum into the “quefrency” domain, turning multiplicative source–path convolutions into additive sums and making the sideband spacing (i.e., f_\text{fault}) directly readable as a peak location.



The real cepstrum is the inverse DFT of the log power spectrum:

c[\tau] = \mathcal{F}^{-1}\!\left\{\ln |\hat{X}(f)|^2\right\}

A family of harmonics spaced \Delta f apart in frequency becomes a single peak at quefrency \tau = 1/\Delta f in the cepstrum. Bearing defect frequencies are thus directly readable without needing to identify individual harmonics.
The liftering operation removes the low-quefrency structural response, isolating the fault signature:

c_\text{liftered}[\tau] = c[\tau] \cdot w[\tau], \quad w[\tau] = \begin{cases} 0 & \tau < \tau_0 \\ 1 & \tau \geq \tau_0 \end{cases}




import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy.io import loadmat

# Load CWRU bearing dataset (48 kHz, drive-end accelerometer)
mat = loadmat('docs/Data/gearbox/CWRU_48k_load_1_CNN_data.npz')
fs = 48_000
x = mat['drive_end_fault'].ravel()[:fs * 4]   # 4-second snippet

# PSD via Welch
f, Pxx = scipy.signal.welch(x, fs=fs, nperseg=4096, scaling='density')

# Real cepstrum
log_psd = np.log(Pxx + 1e-30)
cepstrum = np.fft.irfft(log_psd).real
quefrency = np.arange(len(cepstrum)) / fs * 1e3   # ms

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(9, 6))

axes[0].semilogy(f / 1e3, Pxx)
axes[0].set_xlabel('Frequency (kHz)')
axes[0].set_ylabel('PSD (m²/s⁴/Hz)')
axes[0].set_title('Power Spectrum — bearing fault sidebands')

axes[1].plot(quefrency[1:500], cepstrum[1:500], lw=0.8)
axes[1].set_xlabel('Quefrency (ms)')
axes[1].set_ylabel('Cepstrum amplitude')
axes[1].set_title('Real Cepstrum — fault period visible as peak')

plt.tight_layout()







Cepstrum of gear-box vibration revealing bearing defect quefrency peak



The cepstrum peak at a quefrency corresponding to the ball-pass outer-race frequency is clearly visible, even though the individual sidebands in the power spectrum are hard to count by eye. Liftering above the structural quefrency leaves only the fault signature.



The clearest way to see a fault is to overlay the healthy and faulty recordings. Using the SpectraQuest gear-box dataset shipped with this book (f_s = 66.7 kHz), the fault modulates the gear mesh at the shaft rotation rate (f_\text{shaft}\approx 77 Hz), sprinkling a family of sidebands spaced 77 Hz apart around the mesh harmonics. In the power spectrum (left) the faulty trace sits well above the healthy one and grows a forest of extra sideband peaks; the cepstrum (right) collapses that whole comb into a single rahmonic at quefrency 1/f_\text{shaft}\approx 12.9 ms — which stands markedly taller for the faulty gear precisely because it carries more sidebands.
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy import signal

d = np.load('Data/gearbox_spectraquest.npz', allow_pickle=True)
fs = int(d['fs']); healthy = d['healthy'].astype(float); broken = d['broken'].astype(float)

def analyse(x):
    f, P = signal.welch(x, fs=fs, nperseg=8192, scaling='density')
    c = np.fft.irfft(np.log(P + 1e-30)).real          # real cepstrum
    q = np.arange(c.size) / fs                         # quefrency [s]
    return f, P, q, c

fh, Ph, qh, ch = analyse(healthy)
fb, Pb, qb, cb = analyse(broken)
q_shaft = 1 / 77.3                                     # shaft-rate quefrency (~12.9 ms)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11.2, 3.6), layout='constrained')

band = (fh > 3500) & (fh < 6500)                       # zoom on a mesh-harmonic band
ax[0].semilogy(fh[band], Ph[band], lw=0.8, label='healthy', zorder=3)  # healthy on top
ax[0].semilogy(fb[band], Pb[band], lw=0.8, label='faulty',  zorder=2)
ax[0].set_xlabel('frequency [Hz]'); ax[0].set_ylabel('PSD [arb.]')
ax[0].set_title('power spectrum — mesh sidebands'); ax[0].legend()

m = (qh > 1.2e-3) & (qh < 0.022)
ax[1].plot(qh[m]*1e3, ch[m], lw=0.9, label='healthy', zorder=3)  # healthy on top
ax[1].plot(qb[m]*1e3, cb[m], lw=0.9, label='faulty',  zorder=2)
for k in (1, 2, 3):
    ax[1].axvline(k*q_shaft*1e3, ls=':', lw=0.7, color='0.5')  # shaft rahmonics
ax[1].set_xlabel('quefrency [ms]'); ax[1].set_ylabel('cepstrum amplitude [arb.]')
ax[1].set_title('cepstrum — shaft-rate rahmonic'); ax[1].legend()

plt.savefig('figure_gearbox_cepstrum_compare.png', dpi=200, bbox_inches='tight')




Healthy (blue) vs. faulty (red) gear-box vibration. Left: in a mesh-harmonic band the faulty spectrum lifts above the healthy one and grows extra sidebands spaced at the shaft rate. Right: the cepstrum turns that sideband comb into one rahmonic at 1/f_\text{shaft}\approx 12.9 ms (and its multiples at 6.5 and 19.4 ms) — taller for the faulty gear because it has more sidebands to accumulate.



A single scalar — the height of the shaft-rate rahmonic — thus separates a healthy gear from a faulty one, without having to count sidebands by eye. This mirrors the classic comparison in Siemens’ Cepstrum Analysis tutorial (their Figure 11), reproduced here from this book’s own SpectraQuest data.

See Chapter 2 for the cepstrum definition, liftering, and connection to homomorphic signal processing.

title: Gravitational Waves (GW150914)
text:
← Back to Gallery
Topic: Time–frequency analysis — continuous wavelet transform (Morlet) with an AR(1) significance test. Chapter: 7 — Wavelet & Time-Frequency Analysis



On 14 September 2015 the two LIGO interferometers recorded GW150914, the first direct detection of gravitational waves — two black holes (~36 and ~29 M_\odot) merging ~1.3 billion light-years away. The radiated strain is the textbook chirp: as the binary inspirals, both the amplitude and the frequency sweep upward until the merger, then the remnant rings down.

Inspiral → merger → ringdown: the upward frequency sweep is exactly what a time–frequency method should reveal.



A single Fourier transform smears this non-stationary signal. The recipe instead is: whiten the strain (divide each Fourier bin by the local noise amplitude, flattening the coloured detector noise), take the Morlet continuous wavelet transform, and test the wavelet power against an AR(1) red-noise background — drawing the contour where it exceeds the \chi^2_2 confidence level (Torrence & Compo). The constant-Q wavelet window narrows in time as frequency rises, so it tracks the accelerating chirp far better than a fixed-window STFT.



import numpy as np, urllib.request
import scipy.signal as sig, scipy.interpolate, scipy.stats, ssqueezepy
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt, matplotlib.colors as mcolors
from matplotlib.colors import LinearSegmentedColormap
from matplotlib.collections import LineCollection
from scipy.ndimage import gaussian_filter
from ssqueezepy.experimental import scale_to_freq

fs = 4096; dt = 1 / fs
tm = 16.422; t0 = tm - 0.45                        # window start -> x runs 0..0.5 s

# LIGO Open Science Center strain (4096 Hz, 32 s around GW150914)
base = 'https://gwosc.org/s/events/GW150914/'
def fetch(tag):
    fn = f'{tag}_LOSC_4_V2-1126259446-32.txt.gz'
    urllib.request.urlretrieve(base + fn, fn)
    return np.loadtxt(fn)
H1, L1 = fetch('H-H1'), fetch('L-L1')
t = np.arange(len(H1)) * dt

def whiten(x):
    f, Pxx = sig.welch(x, fs=fs, nperseg=4 * fs)
    psd = scipy.interpolate.interp1d(f, Pxx, bounds_error=False, fill_value=np.inf)
    freqs = np.fft.rfftfreq(len(x), dt)
    return np.fft.irfft(np.fft.rfft(x) / np.sqrt(psd(freqs) / dt / 2.), n=len(x))
bb, ab = sig.butter(4, [30, 350], btype='band', fs=fs)

cmap_H = LinearSegmentedColormap.from_list('H', ['#000000','#2a0f00','#7a2e00','#e0700a','#ffb84d','#fff3d6'])

yc, kk, Sbar = 12.5, 0.038, 5.0
def gradient_line(ax, x, y, color, lw):            # truncated ends fade out in alpha
    a = np.clip((x - x[0]) / 0.05, 0, 1) * np.clip((x[-1] - x) / 0.025, 0, 1)
    pts = np.array([x, y]).T.reshape(-1, 1, 2)

    rgba = np.tile([*mcolors.to_rgb(color), 1.0], (len(seg), 1)); rgba[:, 3] = 0.5*(a[:-1] + a[1:])

fig.subplots_adjust(hspace=0.06, left=0.115, right=0.985, top=0.985, bottom=0.115)

title: Gravitational Waves (GW150914)
text:
On 14 September 2015 the two LIGO interferometers recorded GW150914, the first direct detection of gravitational waves — two black holes (~36 and ~29 M_\odot) merging ~1.3 billion light-years away. The radiated strain is the textbook chirp: as the binary inspirals, both the amplitude and the frequency sweep upward until the merger, then the remnant rings down.

Inspiral → merger → ringdown: the upward frequency sweep is exactly what a time–frequency method should reveal.

title: Gravitational Waves (GW150914)
text: A single Fourier transform smears this non-stationary signal. The recipe instead is: whiten the strain (divide each Fourier bin by the local noise amplitude, flattening the coloured detector noise), take the Morlet continuous wavelet transform, and test the wavelet power against an AR(1) red-noise background — drawing the contour where it exceeds the \chi^2_2 confidence level (Torrence & Compo). The constant-Q wavelet window narrows in time as frequency rises, so it tracks the accelerating chirp far better than a fixed-window STFT.

title: Cosmic Microwave Background
text:
← Back to Gallery
Topic: Angular power spectrum — the Wiener–Khinchin theorem on the 2-sphere, applied to the oldest light in the Universe. Chapter: 3 — Power Spectral Density



The Cosmic Microwave Background is the afterglow of the Big Bang — light released 375,000 years after the beginning, when the Universe first cooled enough for neutral atoms to form. It reaches us as a nearly uniform 2.7 K glow, but imprinted on it are temperature fluctuations of \sim\!100\ \muK: a frozen snapshot of the sound waves that rippled through the primordial plasma.




The Universe’s timeline: quantum fluctuations imprinted at inflation become the CMB “afterglow light pattern” 375,000 years later, then grow into galaxies. Credit: NASA/WMAP Science Team.



Because those fluctuations are a statistically isotropic random field on a sphere, there is no meaningful “value at a point” to predict — only a power spectrum to measure. The natural summary statistic is the angular power spectrum C_\ell: how much temperature variance lives at each angular scale, indexed by multipole \ell (roughly, \theta \approx 180^\circ/\ell).



The two-point correlation function C(\theta) = \langle T(\hat n_1)\,T(\hat n_2)\rangle depends only on the angular separation \theta. The spherical Wiener–Khinchin theorem says its Legendre transform is the power spectrum:

C_\ell = 2\pi \int_{-1}^{1} C(\theta)\, P_\ell(\cos\theta)\, d\cos\theta

the exact angular analogue of S(f) = \mathcal{F}\{R(\tau)\} on the line. This is a definition, not an algorithm: pair-counting C(\theta) over the \sim\!10^{14} pixel pairs of a real sky map is hopeless, so production pipelines evaluate the same sum in harmonic space with healpy.anafast in O(N\ell_{\max}).







Top: a simulated full-sky CMB temperature map (Mollweide projection); the zoom-in circles one acoustic wavelength — \theta\approx360^\circ/\ell\approx1.6^\circ for the first peak (\ell\approx220), set by the baryon-acoustic sound horizon at recombination. Bottom: the same realisation analysed — (a) the two-point correlation C(\theta), with Monte-Carlo pairs scattering about the exact \LambdaCDM curve, and (b) the angular power spectrum, where anafast and the pair-counting Wiener–Khinchin estimator both recover the same acoustic-peak structure of the \LambdaCDM model.



The first acoustic peak at \ell\approx220 sets the scale on which hot and cold patches repeat, \theta\approx360^\circ/\ell\approx1.6^\circ (individual spots span half that) — fixed by the distance a sound wave could travel in the plasma before recombination froze it in. anafast (harmonic transform) and the pair-counting Wiener–Khinchin estimator agree through the first peak — the spherical-geometry version of “Welch and the FT of the autocorrelation give the same PSD”. The pair estimator’s noise grows as \ell^2, so it is a large-angle tool; the harmonic transform carries the high-\ell tail out to the Silk-damping cutoff.



import numpy as np, healpy as hp

# theory LCDM spectrum shipped with healpy -> one full-sky realisation
lmax = 1500; ell = np.arange(lmax + 1)
Dl = np.loadtxt(hp.data.get_data_path() + 'totcls.dat')[:lmax + 1, 1]
Cl_th = np.zeros(lmax + 1); Cl_th[2:] = Dl[2:] * 2 * np.pi / (ell[2:] * (ell[2:] + 1))
cmb_map = hp.synfast(Cl_th, nside=1024, lmax=lmax, pixwin=False)

# Method A — spherical harmonics: the same C_l, computed in O(N l_max)
Cl_A = hp.anafast(cmb_map, lmax=lmax)

# Method B — Wiener-Khinchin: pair-count C(theta), then Legendre-transform
#   C_l = 2*pi * integral C(theta) P_l(cos theta) d(cos theta)

See Chapter 3 for the full three-method derivation, the definition-versus-computation trade-off, and the proof that anafast and pair-counting Wiener–Khinchin evaluate the identical sum.

title: Indian Cuckoo Song
text:
← Back to Gallery
Topic: Short-Time Fourier Transform (STFT) applied to bioacoustics. Chapter: 7 — Time-Frequency Analysis



The Indian Cuckoo (Cuculus micropterus) produces a highly stereotyped four-note call — often described as the phrase “one more bottle”. In the raw pressure waveform the repeated phrase is barely distinguishable by eye. The STFT maps each short frame onto a local spectrum, stacking them into a spectrogram that makes the periodic phrase and the individual note frequencies immediately visible.
The call sits in the 1–3 kHz band. Each note shows a slight downward frequency glide, and the inter-note silences appear as clean gaps in the time-frequency plane.



The STFT of a signal x(t) with analysis window g(t) is

X(\tau, f) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x(t)\, g(t - \tau)\, e^{-j2\pi f t}\, dt

The spectrogram is the squared magnitude |X(\tau, f)|^2, giving instantaneous power as a function of both time and frequency. Window length L sets the time–frequency resolution trade-off: longer windows give finer frequency resolution at the cost of poorer time localisation.



import numpy as np
import scipy.signal
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy.io import wavfile

fs, x = wavfile.read('docs/Data/indian_cuckoo_short.wav')
x = x.astype(float) / np.iinfo(x.dtype).max   # normalise to [-1, 1]

N_window = 4096
window = scipy.signal.windows.hann(N_window, sym=True)
STFT = scipy.signal.ShortTimeFFT(window, hop=128, fs=fs,
                                  scale_to='psd', fft_mode='onesided2X')

Sxx = STFT.spectrogram(x)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(10, 6), sharex=False)

# Waveform
t = np.arange(len(x)) / fs
axes[0].plot(t, x, lw=0.5, color='steelblue')
axes[0].set_ylabel('Amplitude')
axes[0].set_xlabel('Time (s)')

# Spectrogram
t_stft = STFT.t(len(x))
f_stft = STFT.f
axes[1].pcolormesh(t_stft, f_stft / 1e3, 10 * np.log10(Sxx + 1e-12),
                   shading='gouraud', cmap='inferno', vmin=-60, vmax=0)
axes[1].set_ylim(0, 6)
axes[1].set_ylabel('Frequency (kHz)')
axes[1].set_xlabel('Time (s)')

plt.tight_layout()







Indian Cuckoo STFT spectrogram showing four-note phrase structure



The spectrogram reveals the four-note phrase repeating with roughly 0.5 s between calls. Each note occupies ~1.5–2.5 kHz and lasts about 0.2 s. This structure is completely invisible in the waveform alone.

See Chapter 7 for a full treatment of STFT, window choice, and the uncertainty principle.

title: Weighted Summation
text:
Sliding Window
numpy.lib.stride_tricks.sliding_window_view(x, window_shape, axis=None, *, subok=False, writeable=False) provides the function for re-organizing the signal into several sub-chunk. This function can only give a stride of one. For a customized stride, you need to use numpy.lib.stride_tricks.as_strided(x, shape=None, strides=None, subok=False, writeable=True). This function can be unsafe and crash your program.
The bottleneck package, which is safer and more efficient, is more suggested for common usage of moving windows, like moving-average and moving-maximum. The following code shows how to use the bottleneck functions and their expected results.
# -------------------------------
# Method 1: sliding_window_view (fixed stride = 1)
# -------------------------------
window_size = 4
windows_stride1 = sliding_window_view(sig, window_shape=window_size)

# -------------------------------
# Method 2: as_strided (custom stride, use with caution!)
# -------------------------------
custom_stride = 2
n_windows = (len(sig) - window_size) // custom_stride + 1
shape = (n_windows, window_size)
strides = (sig.strides[0] * custom_stride, sig.strides[0])

windows_custom = as_strided(sig, shape=shape, strides=strides)

# -------------------------------
# Method 3: bottleneck (safe, NaN-aware window functions)
# -------------------------------
ma = bn.move_mean(sig, window=3, min_count=1)
mm = bn.move_max(sig, window=3, min_count=1)
std = bn.move_std(sig, window=3, min_count=1)

title: Wavelet and Time-Frequency Analysis
text:
The Short-Time Fourier Transform (STFT) extends traditional Fourier analysis to non-stationary signals by introducing time localization via windowing. This allows us to track how the frequency content of a signal evolves over time. This section explains the trade-off between time and frequency resolution, the role of window functions, and practical implementation with scipy.signal.shortTimeFFT. It should be noted that function scipy.signal.stft is considered legacy and will no longer receive updates. While scipy currently have no plans to remove it, they recommend that new code uses more modern alternatives shortTimeFFT instead. Here is an example of using scipy.signal.ShortTimeFFT to perform STFT on a synthetic signal composed of multiple sine waves with varying frequencies and amplitudes, along with some added noise.
N_window = 4096
N_step = 100

# Hanning Window
window_hann = scipy.signal.windows.hann(N_window, sym = True) 

# create the STFT object
STFT = scipy.signal.ShortTimeFFT(window_hann, hop=N_step, fs = fs, scale_to='psd', fft_mode = 'onesided2X')  

# perform the STFT
psd_stft = STFT.stft(sig)  
time_stft = np.arange(0, psd_stft.shape[1]) * STFT.hop / fs - STFT.win.size / 2 / fs
frequency_stft = np.fft.rfftfreq(window_hann, d=dt)

The STFT spectra of a signal that consists of a growing wave, a chriping wave, and a contant wave.

The red hashed region indicates the cone of influence (COI), which represents the area where edge effects may distort the STFT results due to the finite length of the signal and windowing. The COI is typically defined as half the window length on either side of the time axis, beyond which the STFT results should be interpreted with caution. The affected results is sensitive to the padding method and therefore more subjective. Thus they are often masked out in visualizations to highlight the reliable region of the time-frequency representation.


A spectrogram plots only |S(f,t)| — the STFT magnitude. The phase is discarded, and with it, apparently, the waveform. But an STFT with overlapping windows is redundant: every sample is described by several frames, so the magnitude alone holds more numbers than the signal has samples. Neighbouring frames must agree about the samples they share, and essentially only one phase assignment lets them — the redundancy carries the phase in disguise. The demo below works at 50 % overlap, barely two numbers per sample, to show the recovery succeeding even at half the usual redundancy.
The Griffin–Lim algorithm recovers it by alternating two projections: enforce consistency (inverse-transform, then forward-transform — snap to something a real signal could produce), then restore the given magnitudes (keep only the negotiated phase). Started from random phase, a couple hundred rounds turn noise-phase garbage back into intelligible speech:


FigureCode





import numpy as np, scipy.signal as sig

nper, hop = 1024, 512                      # 50% overlap -> only ~2x redundancy
nov = nper - hop
_, _, S = sig.stft(y, fs, nperseg=nper, noverlap=nov)
A = np.abs(S)                              # the spectrogram: magnitude ONLY

X = A * np.exp(2j*np.pi*np.random.rand(*A.shape))     # start from random phase
for k in range(300):                                  # Griffin-Lim iterations
    _, x  = sig.istft(X, fs, nperseg=nper, noverlap=nov)   # -> signal domain
    _, _, Sx = sig.stft(x, fs, nperseg=nper, noverlap=nov) # -> a CONSISTENT stft
    X = A * np.exp(1j * np.angle(Sx))                 # keep our magnitude
_, x_rec = sig.istft(X, fs, nperseg=nper, noverlap=nov)    # recovered speech




Speech recovered from a magnitude-only spectrogram at 50 % overlap: the waveform at iteration 10 is still noisy; by iteration 300 the frames have negotiated a consistent phase. Overlap is what makes it work — with disjoint frames, any phase is self-consistent and the iteration never improves.

Listen — both clips share the same magnitude spectrogram and differ only in phase:



original


iteration 300recovered from magnitude alone















The same “phase problem” rules X-ray crystallography, where detectors record only |\mathcal{F}\{\rho\}|^2; and every neural vocoder in modern text-to-speech is trained to solve exactly this task — spectrogram in, phase out. See the gallery example for the full derivation, the overlap comparison, and the honest limits.




Although the STFT can represent a signal on the time–frequency plane, it does so with a fixed window: a short window yields good resolution at high frequencies but blurs low-frequency components, while a long window does the opposite—there is no way to optimize both simultaneously.

The wavelet transform turns this static trade-off into an adaptive resolution by scaling its analysis “window” with frequency—long windows for low frequencies and short windows for high frequencies—making it particularly well-suited to multiscale, transient features in non-stationary signals.

Formally, both methods project the signal onto a family of basis functions via inner products: the STFT uses windowed sinusoids as its basis, whereas the continuous wavelet transform replaces the sinusoid with a scalable, time-localized “wavelet.” It is this additional scale parameter that provides the core advantage of wavelet analysis, as we will explore in the next section.
In Python, there are two classic packages for performing continuous wavelet transforms: pywt and ssqueezepy. As shown below, pywt offers a comprehensive set of basic features, while ssqueezepy delivers high computational efficiency and supports synchrosqueezing wavelets. Older versions of Scipy also provided a cwt function, but this functionality has been deprecated in more recent releases.
import pywt
import ssqueezepy

N_per_octave = 12
scales = 2 ** np.linspace(4, 12, 8 * N_per_octave, endpoint = False)

bandwidth = 12.0
central_frequency = 1.0

# pywavelets
wavelet = 'cmor%.1f-%.1f' % (bandwidth, central_frequency)
coef, f = pywt.cwt(sig, scales, wavelet, dt, method = 'fft')
coef *= np.sqrt(np.sqrt(bandwidth) * np.sqrt(2 * np.pi))  # amplitude normalization for Morlet
psd = (np.abs(coef) ** 2) * (2 * dt)
df = (f[0] / f[1] - 1) * f / np.sqrt(f[0] / f[1])

# ssqueezepy
coef, scales = ssqueezepy.cwt(sig, ('morlet', {'mu': bandwidth}), scales = bandwidth / (2 * np.pi) * scales.astype(np.float32), fs = 1 / dt, l1_norm = False)
freq = (bandwidth + np.sqrt(bandwidth ** 2 + 2)) / 2 / (2 * np.pi) / dt / scales
df = (freq[0] / freq[1] - 1) * freq / np.sqrt(freq[0] / freq[1])
psd = (np.abs(coef) ** 2) * (2 * dt)

coi = (np.sqrt(4) * bandwidth / (2 * np.pi) / f).astype(float)
The COI of wavelet is defined as the e-folding time of the wavelet at each scale, which is the time it takes for the wavelet amplitude to decay to 1/e of its maximum value.
Torrence & Compo (1998) give a very impressive summary of the CWT and its application to geophysical time series, which is widely cited in various fields. They recommend using the Morlet wavelet with a non-dimensional frequency \omega_0=6 for general-purpose analysis, as it provides a good balance between time and frequency localization.


Morlet (or Gabor) wavelet is one of the most commonly-used continuous mother wavelet, which has the approximate form of: 
\psi_{approx}(\eta):=\pi^{-1/4} {e^{-{\eta^2}/{2}}} \cdot {e^{i\omega_0\eta}}
 with scale function \eta=s\cdot t where s denotes scale in the large \omega_0 domain.
This mother wavelet is a Gaussian-windowed complex sinusoid, which provides a good balance between time and frequency localization. The parameter \omega_0 is the non-dimensional frequency, which controls the number of oscillations within the Gaussian envelope. A common choice is \omega_0=6, which provides a good trade-off between time and frequency resolution.

On 14 September 2015 the two LIGO interferometers recorded GW150914 — the first direct detection of gravitational waves, radiated by two black holes (~36 and ~29 M_\odot) spiralling together ~1.3 billion light-years away. The signal is the textbook example of a chirp: as the black holes inspiral, both the amplitude and the frequency of the strain sweep upward, until the merger. A single Fourier transform would smear this entirely — it is exactly the non-stationary signal that time–frequency analysis exists to expose.
Physically, the waveform is the binary’s life in three acts:

The two black holes inspiral — the strain’s frequency and amplitude rising together (the chirp) — then merge at peak strain, and the single remnant rings down through damped oscillations to a quiescent Kerr black hole. The upward sweep you read off the wavelet scalogram below is this inspiral; the brief damped tail after the peak is the ringdown.
The raw strain is dominated by the detector’s coloured noise (seismic at low frequency, thermal and shot noise elsewhere), so a real GW pipeline first whitens it — dividing every Fourier bin by the local noise amplitude so that all frequencies carry equal weight — and then band-passes to the sensitive band. With that done, the buried chirp emerges in both detectors at once:






NoteReading the figure




One panel per detector — LIGO Hanford (top) and LIGO Livingston (bottom). Each shows the Morlet-wavelet (CWT) scalogram of that detector’s whitened strain; the band-passed strain itself is drawn as the wiggling line over the time of interest (the last ~0.15 s), and the vertical I-beam at the left gives its amplitude — about 5\sigma of the whitened-noise level.
In both detectors the same bright track sweeps up — from ~35 Hz to past ~250 Hz in the final ~0.2 s — the inspiral chirp, ending at the merger. Two independent instruments, 3000 km apart, recording the identical sweep is the core of the detection’s credibility.
The white outline is the 99.7 % (3\sigma) significance contour: the wavelet power exceeding the \chi^2_2 confidence level of an AR(1) red-noise background (Torrence & Compo). The chirp clears it comfortably in both detectors; essentially nothing in the surrounding noise does.
Because the wavelet’s window narrows in time as the frequency rises (constant-Q), it tracks the rapidly accelerating chirp far more cleanly than a fixed-window STFT could — exactly what the continuous wavelet transform built above is for.



The public strain comes from the Gravitational Wave Open Science Center (GWOSC), 4096 Hz, 32 s around the event.

from matplotlib.colors import LinearSegmentedColormap
from matplotlib.collections import LineCollection
from scipy.ndimage import gaussian_filter
from ssqueezepy.experimental import scale_to_freq

fs = 4096; dt = 1 / fs
tm = 16.422; t0 = tm - 0.45                        # window start -> x runs 0..0.5 s

# --- LIGO Open Science Center strain (4096 Hz, 32 s around GW150914) ---
base = 'https://gwosc.org/s/events/GW150914/'
def fetch(tag):
    fn = f'{tag}_LOSC_4_V2-1126259446-32.txt.gz'
    urllib.request.urlretrieve(base + fn, fn)
    return np.loadtxt(fn)                          # 3 header lines auto-skipped (comments='#')
H1, L1 = fetch('H-H1'), fetch('L-L1')
t = np.arange(len(H1)) * dt

def whiten(x):                                     # flatten the coloured detector noise
    f, Pxx = sig.welch(x, fs=fs, nperseg=4 * fs)
    psd = scipy.interpolate.interp1d(f, Pxx, bounds_error=False, fill_value=np.inf)
    freqs = np.fft.rfftfreq(len(x), dt)
    return np.fft.irfft(np.fft.rfft(x) / np.sqrt(psd(freqs) / dt / 2.), n=len(x))
bb, ab = sig.butter(4, [30, 350], btype='band', fs=fs)

cmap_H = LinearSegmentedColormap.from_list('H', ['#000000','#2a0f00','#7a2e00','#e0700a','#ffb84d','#fff3d6'])
cmap_L = LinearSegmentedColormap.from_list('L', ['#000000','#04132e','#0a3b7a','#1f7fe0','#8fc8ff','#eaf6ff'])

yc, kk, Sbar = 12.5, 0.038, 5.0                    # trace baseline (Hz), log-gain, scale bar (sigma)
def gradient_line(ax, x, y, color, lw):            # line whose truncated ends fade out in alpha
    a = np.clip((x - x[0]) / 0.05, 0, 1) * np.clip((x[-1] - x) / 0.025, 0, 1)
    pts = np.array([x, y]).T.reshape(-1, 1, 2)
    seg = np.concatenate([pts[:-1], pts[1:]], axis=1)
    rgba = np.tile([*mcolors.to_rgb(color), 1.0], (len(seg), 1)); rgba[:, 3] = 0.5*(a[:-1] + a[1:])
    ax.add_collection(LineCollection(seg, colors=rgba, linewidths=lw))

fig.subplots_adjust(hspace=0.06, left=0.115, right=0.985, top=0.985, bottom=0.115)
for ax, raw, cmap, wcol, label in [(axH, H1, cmap_H, '#ff9a2e', 'LIGO Hanford'),
                                   (axL, L1, cmap_L, '#46a6ff', 'LIGO Livingston')]:
    Xw = whiten(raw)
    mw = (t > t0) & (t < tm + 0.05); xw = t[mw] - t0        # 0 .. 0.5 s
    Wx, scales = ssqueezepy.cwt(Xw[mw], ('morlet', {'mu': 6}), fs=fs, l1_norm=False)
    freqs = scale_to_freq(scales, ('morlet', {'mu': 6}), mw.sum(), fs=fs)
    sel = (freqs >= 22) & (freqs <= 512); fr = freqs[sel]; Pw = np.abs(Wx[sel])**2
    ax.pcolormesh(xw, fr, np.sqrt(Pw), shading='gouraud', cmap=cmap,
                  vmax=np.percentile(np.sqrt(Pw)[:, xw > 0.30], 99.6))

    # --- AR(1) red-noise 99% significance contour (Torrence & Compo) ---
    x  = Xw[mw] - Xw[mw].mean()
    a1 = max(np.corrcoef(x[:-1], x[1:])[0, 1], 0.0)              # lag-1 autocorrelation
    Pbg = (1 - a1**2) / (1 + a1**2 - 2*a1*np.cos(2*np.pi*fr/fs)) # red-noise background spectrum
    noise = xw < 0.25
    cal = np.median(Pw[:, noise].mean(1) / Pbg)                 # calibrate amplitude to the noise
    sig = cal * Pbg * scipy.stats.chi2(2).ppf(0.997) / 2        # 99.7% (3 sigma): chi2_2/2 = 5.81
    R = gaussian_filter(Pw, sigma=(1.6, 22.0)) / sig[:, None]
    ax.contour(xw, fr, R, levels=[1.0], colors='w', linewidths=1.0, alpha=0.85)

    # --- whitened strain (sigma units), gradient-faded, over the time of interest ---
    ws = sig.filtfilt(bb, ab, Xw)[mw]; ws = ws / ws[noise].std()
    keep = xw > 0.33
    gradient_line(ax, xw[keep], yc*10**(kk*np.clip(ws[keep], -6, 6)), wcol, 1.9)
    xb = 0.055                                                  # vertical I-beam: amplitude in sigma

    ax.text(xb + 0.018, yc, f'{Sbar:.0f}$\\sigma$', color=wcol, fontsize=12, va='center', ha='left', fontweight='bold')

    ax.set_yticks([8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256, 512]); ax.set_yticklabels([8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256, 512])

The Discrete Wavelet Transform (DWT) decomposes a signal into approximation coefficients (representing low-frequency components that capture the coarse structure) and detail coefficients (representing high-frequency components that capture rapid changes and local details). In contrast to the FFT—which decomposes a signal into sine and cosine functions spanning the entire duration—the DWT breaks the signal into wavelets that are localized in both time and frequency. This inherent multi-resolution analysis enables the DWT to capture transient time-domain information while still revealing its frequency content, effectively offering both temporal and spectral insights.



The decomposition can be iteratively applied, resulting in multi-level DWT, offering multi-resolution analysis. Reconstruction from these coefficients exactly recovers the original signal (except minor numerical errors).

Single-Level DWT Example

Let’s perform single-level decomposition and reconstruction:
import pywt

sig = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]
cA, cD = pywt.dwt(sig, 'db1')  # Haar wavelet

print("Approximation (cA):", cA)
# lessCopyEditApproximation (cA): [2.12, 4.95, 7.78]  

print("Detail (cD):", cD)
# Detail (cD): [-0.71, -0.71, -0.71]

# Reconstruction
reconstructed = pywt.idwt(cA, cD, 'db1')
print("Reconstructed:", reconstructed)
# Reconstructed: [1. 2. 3. 4. 5. 6.]

Multi-Level DWT Example

Multi-level decomposition provides more granular frequency analysis. Here’s a two-level decomposition example:
import pywt

sig = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8]
coeffs = pywt.wavedec(sig, 'db1', level=2)
cA2, cD2, cD1 = coeffs

print("cA2:", cA2)
# cA2: [ 5. 13.]  

print("cD2:", cD2)
# cD2: [-2. -2.]  

print("cD1:", cD1)
# cD1: [-0.71 -0.71 -0.71 -0.71]

reconstructed = pywt.waverec(coeffs, 'db1')
print("Reconstructed:", reconstructed)
# Reconstructed: [1. 2. 3. 4. 5. 6. 7. 8.]
Here, different levels represent signal features at different frequency bands.
Different wavelet families (e.g., Daubechies, Symlets, Coiflets, Biorthogonal) offer various trade-offs in terms of compact support, symmetry, and vanishing moments. The choice of wavelet affects the decomposition quality and should be selected based on the signal characteristics and analysis goals.


Wavelet denoising leverages the idea that noise predominantly appears as low-amplitude coefficients, whereas meaningful signals appear as larger coefficients. We remove noise by applying a threshold to detail coefficients, retaining major signal features.
Two common thresholding methods:

Hard Thresholding: Sets coefficients smaller than threshold to zero, others remain unchanged (may cause discontinuities).
Soft Thresholding: Smoothly reduces coefficients above the threshold towards zero (creates smoother results).

We generate a noisy sinusoidal signal and denoise it using soft thresholding.
Steps:

Decompose signal using DWT.
Estimate noise level \sigma from detail coefficients and compute threshold: 
T = \sigma \sqrt{2\ln(N)}

Apply soft thresholding to detail coefficients.
Reconstruct the denoised signal.

2-dimensional DWT allows the scale decomposition for a 2-D object like an image. Its key advantage is the ability to perform multi-resolution analysis by breaking down the image into different frequency subbands. Typically, the 2D-DWT decomposes an image into one approximation subband (LL, or cA, for Approximated coefficient) that captures the coarse, low-frequency components, and three detail subbands (LH, HL, HH) that represent horizontal, vertical, and diagonal high-frequency details respectively. This decomposition not only facilitates efficient image compression by isolating and quantizing the less perceptually significant high-frequency details, but it also aids in tasks such as denoising and feature extraction, where preserving both spatial and spectral information is critical.
Worked example. We compress an 8-bit grey-scale photograph by replacing every detail coefficient whose magnitude is below a percentile-based threshold with zero, then reconstructing. Sweeping the threshold from 0\% (lossless) to 99\% (only the top 1\% of coefficients kept) traces out a rate-distortion curve: how many coefficients we keep versus the resulting peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR).
The Daubechies-4 (db4) basis is a good default — compactly supported, four vanishing moments, and orthogonal so the energy at each level is preserved. With 95\% of the coefficients zeroed the picture is still visually faithful, illustrating the strong sparsity that wavelet bases expose in natural images. This same principle underlies the wavelet-based JPEG-2000 codec.
import pywt

image = scipy.datasets.ascent().astype(float)        # 512x512 sample image

wavelet, level = 'db4', 4
coeffs        = pywt.wavedec2(image, wavelet=wavelet, level=level)
arr, slices   = pywt.coeffs_to_array(coeffs)

ratios = [0.0, 0.5, 0.9, 0.95, 0.99]                 # fraction of coeffs zeroed
psnrs  = []
for r in ratios:
    if r == 0.0:
        arr_c = arr.copy()
    else:
        thresh = np.quantile(np.abs(arr), r)
        arr_c  = np.where(np.abs(arr) >= thresh, arr, 0.0)
    coeffs_c    = pywt.array_to_coeffs(arr_c, slices, output_format='wavedec2')
    image_recon = pywt.waverec2(coeffs_c, wavelet=wavelet)[: image.shape[0], : image.shape[1]]
    mse  = np.mean((image - image_recon) ** 2)
    psnr = 10.0 * np.log10((image.max() ** 2) / max(mse, 1e-12))
    psnrs.append(psnr)

The story starts with the Gabor window (1946), a Gaussian-modulated sinusoid that set the benchmark for joint time–frequency resolution. Early-1980s geophysics added explicit scale, giving the Morlet wavelet—the work-horse of the continuous wavelet transform (CWT). Shortly after, the real, symmetric Mexican-Hat (second derivative of a Gaussian) became popular for edge and peak detection, while Paul wavelets generalized higher-order Gaussian derivatives for finer phase tracking. In 1986 Yves Meyer produced the first rigorously admissible CWT mother, compact in the frequency domain. Finally, band-limited designs such as the Shannon and frequency-B-spline wavelets (early 1990s) offered idealized rectangular spectra for theoreticians and filter-bank designers.









Wavelet Name
Brief Description
Key Properties
Function/Scale Expression




Complex Gaussian (cgau)
Complex-valued derivatives of a Gaussian function; higher order means more oscillations.
Good time-frequency localization; complex-valued; infinite support.
\psi(t) = C \frac{d^n}{dt^n}(e^{-t^2})


Complex Morlet (cmor)
Gaussian-windowed complex sinusoid; useful for capturing phase information and oscillations.
Excellent time-frequency balance; complex-valued; infinite support.
\psi(t) = C e^{-t^2/(2\sigma^2)} e^{i2\pi f_c t}


Morlet (morl)
Real-valued Gaussian-windowed sinusoid, widely used for general analysis.
Good time-frequency localization; infinite support.
\psi(t) = \pi^{-1/4} e^{-t^2/2} \cos(\omega_0 t)


Frequency B-Spline (fbsp)
Band-limited complex wavelet defined by frequency-domain B-splines.
Adjustable bandwidth and smoothness; complex-valued; infinite support.
Defined in frequency domain by B-spline filters.


Mexican Hat (mexh)
Real-valued second derivative of Gaussian; bell-shaped wavelet for edge detection.
Good localization; real-valued; infinite support.
\psi(t) = (1 - t^2) e^{-t^2/2}


Shannon (shan)
Ideal rectangular band-pass wavelet; perfectly band-limited in frequency domain.
Ideal frequency localization; poor time localization; complex-valued; infinite support.
Frequency domain rectangular function; inverse FT yields sinc function.


Gaussian (gaus)
Real-valued Gaussian derivatives (DOG); higher orders mean more oscillations.
Good localization for feature detection; real-valued; infinite support.
\psi(t) = \frac{d^n}{dt^n}(e^{-t^2/2})

The discrete lineage begins with the step-like Haar basis (1910). Jan-Olov Strömberg’s 1983 work showed how to sample continuous wavelets without losing orthogonality, paving the way for Ingrid Daubechies’ breakthrough (1988): compactly supported, arbitrarily smooth orthonormal wavelets (db N). Compression soon demanded linear phase, so biorthogonal pairs appeared—the 5/3 tap Le Gall–Tabatabai (1988) for loss-less, and the longer 9/7 Cohen–Daubechies–Feauveau (1992) for lossy JPEG 2000. Stéphane Mallat’s pyramidal algorithm and subsequent wavelet-packet extension (late 1980s–1990) made \mathcal{O}(N) multiresolution analysis practical. Symlets and Coiflets fine-tuned phase and moment symmetry, and Wim Sweldens’ lifting scheme (1995) recast any biorthogonal filter bank as fast, in-place, integer arithmetic—ideal for hardware codecs.









Wavelet Name
Brief Description
Key Properties
Scale Recurrence Relation




Daubechies (db)
Orthonormal wavelets with compact support; “db1” is Haar wavelet. Higher orders smoother, longer filters.
Orthogonal; asymmetric (except db1); compact support.
\phi(t) = \sqrt{2} \sum_{k} h[k] \phi(2t - k)


Symlets (sym)
Modified Daubechies wavelets with improved symmetry, reducing phase distortion.
Orthogonal; near-symmetric; compact support.
\phi(t) = \sqrt{2} \sum_{k} h[k] \phi(2t - k)


Coiflets (coif)
Designed for equal vanishing moments in scaling and wavelet functions; smoother approximation.
Orthogonal; near-symmetric; compact support.
\phi(t) = \sqrt{2} \sum_{k} h[k] \phi(2t - k)


Biorthogonal (bior & rbio)
Uses separate wavelets for analysis and synthesis, forming dual bases; symmetric filters with linear phase.
Biorthogonal; symmetric; compact support.
\phi_d(t) = \sqrt{2} \sum_{k} h_d[k] \phi_d(2t - k), \phi_r(t) = \sqrt{2} \sum_{k} h_r[k] \phi_r(2t - k)


Discrete Meyer (dmey)
Finite approximation of the Meyer wavelet, with excellent smoothness and frequency characteristics.
Orthonormal; nearly symmetric; finite approximation.
Defined by frequency domain filter approximation.

In the above descriptions on the wavelet functions, several key properties of wavelets are frequently mentioned. Here’s a brief explanation of these terms:

Vanishing Moments (p): The number of moments (derivatives) that vanish at zero, indicating how well the wavelet can represent polynomial functions. 
M_k=\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} t^k \psi(t) dt = 0 \quad \text{for } k = 0, 1, \ldots, p-1


M_p=\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} t^p \psi(t) dt \neq 0

Orthonormal: Wavelets that form an orthogonal basis with unit norm, useful for efficient reconstruction without redundancy. 
\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} \psi_i(t) \psi_j(t) dt = \delta_{ij}

Bi-orthogonal: Involves two wavelet sets forming dual bases, one set for analysis and another for synthesis; allows symmetric filters and linear phase. 
\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} \phi_{d,i}(t) \psi_{r,j}(t) dt = \delta_{ij}\\
  \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} \phi_{r,i}(t) \psi_{d,j}(t) dt = \delta_{ij}

Support: The region in time where the wavelet is non-zero.

Infinite Support: Wavelets extending indefinitely in time, typically with exponential or Gaussian decay.
Finite Support: Wavelets explicitly confined within a finite time interval, completely vanishing outside this interval.






If you want to go deeper into the Morlet wavelet, here are some additional details, which could be especially useful for understanding its properties and applications:

Admissibility: The strict form of Morlet wavelet should satisfy the admissibility condition, which requires the wavelet to have zero mean. However, the standard Morlet wavelet does not strictly satisfy this condition because


\begin{align*}
\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} \psi_{approx}(\eta) \mathrm{d}\eta &= \sqrt{2}\pi^{1/4} e^{-\omega_0^2/2}\\
&= \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} \boxed{\pi^{-1/4}e^{-\omega_0^2/2}e^{-\eta^2/2}} \mathrm{d}\eta = \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} \delta\psi(\eta) \mathrm{d}\eta\\
&\neq 0
\end{align*}

​ To address this, a correction term is often subtracted to ensure zero mean. 
\psi_{adm}(\eta)=\psi_{approx}(\eta)-\delta\psi(\eta)=\pi^{-1/4}e^{-\eta^2/2}\left[e^{i\omega_0\eta}-e^{-\omega_0^2/2}\right]


Normalization: To ensure the corrected morlet wavelet has unit energy, we normalize it so that its L2 norm equals 1. The normalization factor is given by the inverse of the square root of the integral of the squared magnitude of the wavelet.


\psi(\eta)=\frac{\psi_{adm}}{\left[{\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} [\psi^\prime(\eta)]^2 \mathrm{d}\eta}\right]^{-1/2}}=c_{\omega_0}\psi_{adm} = \boxed{\left(1+e^{-\omega_0^2}-2e^{-\frac{3}{4}\omega_0^2}\right)^{-{1}/{2}}}\psi_{adm}

The Final form of Morlet wavelet is: 
\psi(\eta)=ta)={\left(1+e^{-\omega_0^2}-2e^{-\frac{3}{4}\omega_0^2}\right)^{-{1}/{2}}}\pi^{-1/4}e^{-\eta^2/2}\left[e^{i\omega_0\eta}-e^{-\omega_0^2/2}\right]
 when \omega_0\geq 5, the correction term e^{-\omega_0^2/2} is negligible, and the approximate form \psi_{approx} is often used directly.

Frequency Response: Another issue that must be considered is the frequency response of the corrected Morlet wavelet, which is no longer a simple Gaussian centered at \omega_0. Instead, it has a more complex shape due to the subtraction of the correction term:


\hat{\psi}(\omega)=c_{\omega_0}\pi^{-1/4}\left[e^{-(\omega-\omega_0)^2/2}-e^{-\omega_0^2/2}e^{-\omega^2/2}\right]

This affects the relationship between scale and equivalent Fourier period, as well as the central frequency of the wavelet.

Equivalent Fourier Period: For Morlet wavelets with a small \omega_0, the Gaussian envelope e^{-\eta^2/2} dominates over the carrier oscillation e^{-i\omega_0\eta}. As a result, the CWT power spectrum of an input sine wave no longer peaks at the naive period T = 2\pi/\omega_0. Instead, its maximum shifts to the equivalent Fourier period T_{\mathrm{eq}}, which more accurately captures the signal’s power distribution in the frequency domain. 
\begin{align*}
s=\arg\max_s \left|\hat{\psi}\left(\frac{2\pi s}{T_{eq}}\right)\right|\\
\end{align*}
 The equivalent Fourier period can be found by solving the equation:

title: Wavelet and Time-Frequency Analysis
text:
The Short-Time Fourier Transform (STFT) extends traditional Fourier analysis to non-stationary signals by introducing time localization via windowing. This allows us to track how the frequency content of a signal evolves over time. This section explains the trade-off between time and frequency resolution, the role of window functions, and practical implementation with scipy.signal.shortTimeFFT. It should be noted that function scipy.signal.stft is considered legacy and will no longer receive updates. While scipy currently have no plans to remove it, they recommend that new code uses more modern alternatives shortTimeFFT instead. Here is an example of using scipy.signal.ShortTimeFFT to perform STFT on a synthetic signal composed of multiple sine waves with varying frequencies and amplitudes, along with some added noise.
N_window = 4096
N_step = 100

# Hanning Window
window_hann = scipy.signal.windows.hann(N_window, sym = True) 

# create the STFT object
STFT = scipy.signal.ShortTimeFFT(window_hann, hop=N_step, fs = fs, scale_to='psd', fft_mode = 'onesided2X')  

# perform the STFT
psd_stft = STFT.stft(sig)  
time_stft = np.arange(0, psd_stft.shape[1]) * STFT.hop / fs - STFT.win.size / 2 / fs
frequency_stft = np.fft.rfftfreq(window_hann, d=dt)

The STFT spectra of a signal that consists of a growing wave, a chriping wave, and a contant wave.

The red hashed region indicates the cone of influence (COI), which represents the area where edge effects may distort the STFT results due to the finite length of the signal and windowing. The COI is typically defined as half the window length on either side of the time axis, beyond which the STFT results should be interpreted with caution. The affected results is sensitive to the padding method and therefore more subjective. Thus they are often masked out in visualizations to highlight the reliable region of the time-frequency representation.


A spectrogram plots only |S(f,t)| — the STFT magnitude. The phase is discarded, and with it, apparently, the waveform. But an STFT with overlapping windows is redundant: every sample is described by several frames, so the magnitude alone holds more numbers than the signal has samples. Neighbouring frames must agree about the samples they share, and essentially only one phase assignment lets them — the redundancy carries the phase in disguise. The demo below works at 50 % overlap, barely two numbers per sample, to show the recovery succeeding even at half the usual redundancy.
The Griffin–Lim algorithm recovers it by alternating two projections: enforce consistency (inverse-transform, then forward-transform — snap to something a real signal could produce), then restore the given magnitudes (keep only the negotiated phase). Started from random phase, a couple hundred rounds turn noise-phase garbage back into intelligible speech:


FigureCode





import numpy as np, scipy.signal as sig

nper, hop = 1024, 512                      # 50% overlap -> only ~2x redundancy
nov = nper - hop
_, _, S = sig.stft(y, fs, nperseg=nper, noverlap=nov)
A = np.abs(S)                              # the spectrogram: magnitude ONLY

X = A * np.exp(2j*np.pi*np.random.rand(*A.shape))     # start from random phase
for k in range(300):                                  # Griffin-Lim iterations
    _, x  = sig.istft(X, fs, nperseg=nper, noverlap=nov)   # -> signal domain
    _, _, Sx = sig.stft(x, fs, nperseg=nper, noverlap=nov) # -> a CONSISTENT stft
    X = A * np.exp(1j * np.angle(Sx))                 # keep our magnitude
_, x_rec = sig.istft(X, fs, nperseg=nper, noverlap=nov)    # recovered speech




Speech recovered from a magnitude-only spectrogram at 50 % overlap: the waveform at iteration 10 is still noisy; by iteration 300 the frames have negotiated a consistent phase. Overlap is what makes it work — with disjoint frames, any phase is self-consistent and the iteration never improves.

Listen — both clips share the same magnitude spectrogram and differ only in phase:



original


iteration 300recovered from magnitude alone















The same “phase problem” rules X-ray crystallography, where detectors record only |\mathcal{F}\{\rho\}|^2; and every neural vocoder in modern text-to-speech is trained to solve exactly this task — spectrogram in, phase out. See the gallery example for the full derivation, the overlap comparison, and the honest limits.

title: Wavelet and Time-Frequency Analysis
text:
Although the STFT can represent a signal on the time–frequency plane, it does so with a fixed window: a short window yields good resolution at high frequencies but blurs low-frequency components, while a long window does the opposite—there is no way to optimize both simultaneously.

ax.set_title('CWT', pad=10, **title_font)
ax.set_xlim(0, 1); ax.set_ylim(0, 1)
ax.set_xlabel('Time'); ax.set_ylabel('Frequency')
ax.annotate('', xy=(1, 0), xycoords='axes fraction', xytext=(0, 0),
            arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle='->', lw=2, mutation_scale=15))

            arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle='->', lw=2, mutation_scale=15))

ax.spines['bottom'].set_visible(False); ax.spines['left'].set_visible(False)
ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([])

# 以 4 个尺度为例：低频（i=0）1 个宽窗口→高频（i=3）8 个窄窗口
n_scales = 6
for i in range(n_scales):
    y0 = i / n_scales
    band_h = 1 / n_scales
    n_win = 2 ** i
    for k in range(n_win):
        rect = patches.Rectangle((k/n_win, y0), 1/n_win, band_h,
                                 fill=False, edgecolor='black', linewidth=1)
        ax.add_patch(rect)

# Add an arrow and annotation on the right side of axes[1]
axes[1].annotate('', xy=(0.95, 0.9), xycoords='axes fraction',
                    xytext=(.95, 0.05), textcoords='axes fraction',
                    arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle='->', lw=2, mutation_scale=15, color='red'),
                    ha='center', va='center', fontsize=12, color='red', rotation=90)
axes[1].text(1.03, 0.475, 'Higher Frequency\nShorter Window', color='red', rotation = 90, va = 'center', ha = 'center',
             fontsize=12, transform=axes[1].transAxes)
axes[0].annotate('', xy=(0.95, 0.9), xycoords='axes fraction',
                    xytext=(.95, 0.05), textcoords='axes fraction',
                    arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle='->', lw=2, mutation_scale=15, color='blue'),
                    ha='center', va='center', fontsize=12, color='blue', rotation=90)
axes[0].text(1.03, 0.475, 'Fixed Window\nSize', color='blue', rotation=90, va='center', ha='center',
                fontsize=12, transform=axes[0].transAxes)

axes[0].set_xlim(0, 1.1)
axes[0].set_ylim(0, 1.1)

plt.show()



The wavelet transform turns this static trade-off into an adaptive resolution by scaling its analysis “window” with frequency—long windows for low frequencies and short windows for high frequencies—making it particularly well-suited to multiscale, transient features in non-stationary signals.


FigureCode





import pywt
import ssqueezepy

plt.close()
plt.figure(figsize=(8, 6))
plt.subplots_adjust(hspace = 0.02, right = 0.82, left = 0.18)

ax1 = plt.subplot(3, 1, 1)
ax2 = plt.subplot(3, 1, 2, sharex=ax1, sharey = ax1)
ax3 = plt.subplot(3, 1, 3, sharex=ax1)

t = np.linspace(0, 1, N)
dt = t[1] - t[0]

omega = 250

B = 16

wavelet = 'cmor%.1f-%.1f' % (bandwidth, central_frequency)

coef *= np.sqrt(np.sqrt(bandwidth) * np.sqrt(2 * np.pi))  # amplitude normalization for Morlet

mu = np.pi * np.sqrt(2 * B)
# coef, scales = ssqueezepy.cwt(sig, ('morlet', {'mu': bandwidth}), scales = bandwidth / (2 * np.pi) * scales.astype(np.float32), fs = 1 / dt, l1_norm = False)
coef, scales = ssqueezepy.cwt(sig, ('morlet', {'mu': mu}), nv = 20, fs = 1 / dt, l1_norm = False, scales = 'log')
freq = bandwidth / (2 * np.pi) / dt / scales

# integrated_stft_psd = np.nansum((stft_psd.T * df), axis=1)
# ax3.plot(stft_time, integrated_stft_psd, 'C1', label='STFT')

# Theoretical PSD defined as half of the sum of the square of amplitudes of the components
ax3.plot(t, np.ones_like(t) * (3 ** 2 + (16 * t) ** 2 + 6 ** 2 + 2 * noise_level ** 2) / 2, 'k--', label=r'$\frac{1}{2}{\mathrm{Amp_{w}^2} + \sigma_{noise}^2}$')

# ax1.set_xlim(0, 1)

ax3.set_ylim(-5, 240)

ax2.text(0.08, 600, 'ssqueezepy', color = 'w', fontsize = 14, path_effects = path_effect, weight = 'bold', fontstyle = 'italic')

plt.setp(ax1.get_xticklabels(), visible=False)
plt.setp(ax2.get_xticklabels(), visible=False)

    [ax2.get_position().x1 + 0.01, ax2.get_position().y0, 0.02, ax1.get_position().y1 - ax2.get_position().y0])

# cbar2.ax.xaxis.set_ticks([])
