title: AO–Baltic Coherence
text:
← Back to Gallery
Topic: Cross-spectral coherence — identifying coupled oscillation modes between two geophysical time series. Chapter: 8 — Multi-Channel Signals



The Arctic Oscillation (AO) index measures the strength of the polar vortex; a positive AO corresponds to a strong vortex that confines cold Arctic air. The Baltic Sea ice extent responds to large-scale atmospheric forcing, but is also modulated by local temperature and sea-surface salinity. Cross-spectral coherence tests whether the two series share significant variance at specific frequencies — a necessary (though not sufficient) condition for a physical link.
Both records span roughly 1900–present at monthly resolution, placing the analysis in the 2–15 year interannual band.



The magnitude-squared coherence between two zero-mean stationary processes x and y is

C_{xy}(f) = \frac{|S_{xy}(f)|^2}{S_{xx}(f)\, S_{yy}(f)}, \quad 0 \le C_{xy}(f) \le 1

where S_{xy}(f) = \mathbb{E}[\hat{X}^*(f)\hat{Y}(f)] is the cross-power spectral density. A value near 1 means the two signals are linearly related at that frequency; a value near 0 means they are independent. The phase spectrum \angle S_{xy}(f) gives the phase lag.
Significance level for K averaged segments: a coherence value exceeds the 1-\alpha threshold when

C_{xy}(f) > 1 - \alpha^{1/(K-1)}




import numpy as np
import scipy.signal
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# Monthly AO index (NOAA) and Baltic ice extent (SMHI)
ao   = np.loadtxt('docs/Data/jao.txt',     usecols=1)
ice  = np.loadtxt('docs/Data/jbaltic.txt', usecols=1)

# Align and de-trend both records
n = min(len(ao), len(ice))
ao, ice = scipy.signal.detrend(ao[:n]), scipy.signal.detrend(ice[:n])

fs = 12.0   # samples per year

# Welch cross-spectral density
f, Cxy = scipy.signal.coherence(ao, ice, fs=fs,
                                 window='hann',
                                 nperseg=fs * 20,     # 20-year segments
                                 noverlap=fs * 10)

# Cross-power phase
_, Pxy = scipy.signal.csd(ao, ice, fs=fs,
                           window='hann',
                           nperseg=fs * 20,
                           noverlap=fs * 10)
phase = np.angle(Pxy, deg=True)

# Significance threshold (K ≈ 5 segments, 95 %)
K = int(n / (fs * 20 * 0.5))
sig_95 = 1.0 - 0.05 ** (1.0 / (K - 1))

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(9, 6), sharex=True)

period = 1.0 / f[1:]
axes[0].semilogx(period, Cxy[1:], lw=1.2)
axes[0].axhline(sig_95, color='C1', ls='--', label=f'95 % sig. ({sig_95:.2f})')
axes[0].set_ylabel('Coherence')
axes[0].set_ylim(0, 1)
axes[0].legend()

axes[1].semilogx(period, phase[1:], lw=1.0)
axes[1].set_xlabel('Period (years)')
axes[1].set_ylabel('Phase (°)')
axes[1].set_xlim(1, 50)

plt.tight_layout()







Coherence and phase spectrum between AO index and Baltic Sea ice extent



Statistically significant coherence appears at periods of 6–8 years and ~14 years, with the Baltic ice lagging the AO by roughly 90°. These bands are candidates for physically coupled interannual variability driven by the North Atlantic Oscillation.

See Chapter 8 for cross-spectral density, coherence estimation, and multi-channel signal decomposition.

title: DWT Image Compression
text:
← Back to Gallery
Topic: Discrete Wavelet Transform — multi-resolution image compression by nonlinear coefficient thresholding. Chapter: 7 — Time-Frequency Analysis



Image compression works because natural images are sparse in the right basis: a handful of coefficients carry almost all the energy, and the rest can be thrown away. The Discrete Wavelet Transform (DWT) — the engine behind JPEG 2000 — transforms the whole image into a multi-resolution pyramid where this is dramatically true. Keep only the largest coefficients, invert the transform, and you have a compressed image whose quality degrades gracefully as you keep fewer and fewer.



The 2-D DWT applies a low-pass / high-pass filter pair along rows then columns, producing four subbands per level — LL (approximation), LH / HL / HH (horizontal / vertical / diagonal detail) — and recurses on the LL band. Compression is nonlinear approximation: keep only the largest-magnitude coefficients and zero the rest,

c_\lambda[k] = \begin{cases} c[k] & |c[k]| \geq \lambda \\ 0 & |c[k]| < \lambda \end{cases},

choosing the threshold \lambda so that only a small fraction of coefficients survive. Because wavelet coefficients are localised in space and scale, an edge is captured by a few coefficients near it — so even at high compression the error is a gentle blur (plus faint ringing), not the 8×8 tiling that block-DCT codecs like JPEG suffer.



import numpy as np
import pywt, zlib
from skimage import data

img = data.camera().astype(float) / 255.0            # 512×512 grayscale in [0,1]
H, W = img.shape
raw = H * W                                          # uncompressed 8-bpp size = 256 KB

coeffs = pywt.wavedec2(img, 'db4', level=5)          # transform the whole image
arr, slices = pywt.coeffs_to_array(coeffs)           # all subbands in one array

def compress(keep):                                  # keep = fraction of coefficients retained
    thr = np.percentile(np.abs(arr), 100*(1 - keep))
    kept = np.where(np.abs(arr) >= thr, arr, 0.0)     # hard-threshold: drop the small coefficients
    scale = 2047 / np.abs(kept).max()                 # 12-bit quantise the survivors
    q = np.round(kept * scale).astype(np.int16)
    nbytes = len(zlib.compress(q.tobytes(), 9))       # entropy-code the sparse coefficient array
    rec = pywt.waverec2(pywt.array_to_coeffs(q/scale, slices, 'wavedec2'), 'db4')
    return np.clip(rec[:H, :W], 0, 1), nbytes

for keep in (0.10, 0.02, 0.005):
    rec, nbytes = compress(keep)
    print(f'keep {100*keep:4.1f}%   {nbytes/1024:5.1f} KB   {raw/nbytes:.0f}x smaller')







Wavelet image compression at three sizes. The original (512×512, 8 bpp — 256 KB) followed by db4-wavelet reconstructions keeping 10 %, 2 %, and 0.5 % of the coefficients, stored at 47 KB, 14 KB, and 4.3 KB. Quality degrades gracefully: the 47 KB version is indistinguishable, 14 KB softens slightly, and even the 4.3 KB version stays fully recognisable, blurring and faintly ringing rather than breaking into blocks.



The raw image is 256 KB (512×512 pixels at 8 bits each). Keeping the largest 10 % of the wavelet coefficients stores it in 47 KB — 5× smaller, and visually indistinguishable, because almost all the image’s energy lives in that top tenth. Keep 2 % and it drops to 14 KB (19×), softening only in the fine texture of grass and buildings. Push to 0.5 % — one coefficient in two hundred — and it fits in 4.3 KB (60×); the image finally degrades visibly, but notice how: it blurs and rings gently around edges while staying perfectly recognisable, with none of the abrupt 8×8 tiling that a block-DCT codec (JPEG) shows at the same size. That localisation-in-scale is exactly why wavelet coders like JPEG 2000 and the Mars-rover ICER codec hold up so well at aggressive compression.
The sizes here are real: the surviving coefficients are 12-bit quantised and entropy-coded (zlib), and each image shown is decoded back from exactly those bytes. A production codec (bit-plane coding, a perceptual quantisation matrix) would do better still — but the energy-compaction story this isolates is the heart of why the DWT compresses so well.

See Chapter 7 for the DWT filter-bank construction, the Mallat algorithm, and wavelet-family selection.

title: STFT vs. CWT
text:
← Back to Gallery
Topic: Fixed-resolution vs. adaptive-resolution time-frequency analysis — STFT and CWT on a chirp signal. Chapter: 7 — Time-Frequency Analysis



Both the STFT and the Continuous Wavelet Transform (CWT) decompose a signal into a two-dimensional time-frequency (or time-scale) representation. Their key difference is the resolution trade-off:

The STFT uses a fixed-length window, giving constant time and frequency resolution at all frequencies.
The CWT dilates and translates a mother wavelet, giving wide windows (good frequency resolution) at low frequencies and narrow windows (good time resolution) at high frequencies.

This adaptive behaviour makes the CWT naturally suited to signals like speech, seismic records, or chirps, where transients at high frequency must be localised while low-frequency oscillations are tracked over long durations.



The CWT of x(t) with mother wavelet \psi is

W(a, b) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{a}} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x(t)\, \psi^*\!\left(\frac{t - b}{a}\right) dt

where a > 0 is the scale (inversely related to frequency) and b is the translation (time centre). The Morlet wavelet \psi(t) = e^{j\omega_0 t} e^{-t^2/2} gives an approximate frequency f \approx \omega_0 / (2\pi a).
The Heisenberg uncertainty principle limits the product of time and frequency resolutions:

\Delta t \cdot \Delta f \geq \frac{1}{4\pi}

The STFT uses a constant \Delta t and \Delta f; the CWT trades them adaptively across scales.



import numpy as np
import scipy.signal
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fs = 1000.0
t = np.arange(0, 2.0, 1.0 / fs)
# Linear chirp: 10 Hz at t=0 to 200 Hz at t=2
x = scipy.signal.chirp(t, f0=10, f1=200, t1=2.0, method='linear')
x += 0.3 * np.random.default_rng(42).standard_normal(len(x))

# --- STFT (fixed window) ---
N_win = 256
window = scipy.signal.windows.hann(N_win, sym=True)
STFT_obj = scipy.signal.ShortTimeFFT(window, hop=8, fs=fs,
                                      scale_to='psd', fft_mode='onesided2X')
Sxx = STFT_obj.spectrogram(x)

# --- CWT (Morlet) ---
widths = np.logspace(np.log10(fs / 200), np.log10(fs / 5), 200)
cwtmatr, freqs_cwt = scipy.signal.cwt(x, scipy.signal.morlet2,
                                       widths, w=6, fs=fs)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 5))

axes[0].pcolormesh(STFT_obj.t(len(x)), STFT_obj.f,
                   10 * np.log10(Sxx + 1e-12),
                   shading='gouraud', cmap='magma', vmin=-40)
axes[0].set_xlabel('Time (s)')
axes[0].set_ylabel('Frequency (Hz)')
axes[0].set_title('STFT (fixed window, N=256)')

title: STFT vs. CWT
text:
Both the STFT and the Continuous Wavelet Transform (CWT) decompose a signal into a two-dimensional time-frequency (or time-scale) representation. Their key difference is the resolution trade-off:

The STFT uses a fixed-length window, giving constant time and frequency resolution at all frequencies.
The CWT dilates and translates a mother wavelet, giving wide windows (good frequency resolution) at low frequencies and narrow windows (good time resolution) at high frequencies.

This adaptive behaviour makes the CWT naturally suited to signals like speech, seismic records, or chirps, where transients at high frequency must be localised while low-frequency oscillations are tracked over long durations.

title: STFT vs. CWT
text:
The CWT of x(t) with mother wavelet \psi is

W(a, b) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{a}} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x(t)\, \psi^*\!\left(\frac{t - b}{a}\right) dt

where a > 0 is the scale (inversely related to frequency) and b is the translation (time centre). The Morlet wavelet \psi(t) = e^{j\omega_0 t} e^{-t^2/2} gives an approximate frequency f \approx \omega_0 / (2\pi a).
The Heisenberg uncertainty principle limits the product of time and frequency resolutions:

\Delta t \cdot \Delta f \geq \frac{1}{4\pi}

The STFT uses a constant \Delta t and \Delta f; the CWT trades them adaptively across scales.

title: STFT vs. CWT
text:
import numpy as np
import scipy.signal
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fs = 1000.0
t = np.arange(0, 2.0, 1.0 / fs)
# Linear chirp: 10 Hz at t=0 to 200 Hz at t=2
x = scipy.signal.chirp(t, f0=10, f1=200, t1=2.0, method='linear')
x += 0.3 * np.random.default_rng(42).standard_normal(len(x))

# --- STFT (fixed window) ---

                                       widths, w=6, fs=fs)

axes[0].pcolormesh(STFT_obj.t(len(x)), STFT_obj.f,

title: The Missing Fundamental
text:
← Back to Gallery
Topic: Pitch perception, harmonic structure, and the cepstrum — why a tone keeps its pitch even when its fundamental frequency is deleted. Chapter: 2 — Frequency Domain



Play a middle C (C4) on a piano and you hear a pitch at its fundamental, f_1 \approx 261.6 Hz, coloured by a comb of harmonics 2f_1, 3f_1, 4f_1, \dots. Now delete that fundamental entirely — remove all energy at f_1 and keep only the harmonics — and something surprising happens: the pitch does not change. You still hear the same C4. This is the missing fundamental (also called residue pitch or virtual pitch).
It is not a laboratory curiosity — you hear it constantly:

A telephone passes only \sim\!300–3400 Hz, cutting the \sim\!100–150 Hz fundamental of a male voice, yet the voice keeps its pitch.
Laptop and phone speakers cannot physically move enough air to reproduce bass notes, but music still sounds like it has a bass line.
Pipe-organ builders exploit it deliberately (the resultant bass): two higher pipes create the sensation of a much lower note that no pipe actually sounds.




The pitch we perceive tracks the periodicity of the waveform, not the presence of energy at f_1. A harmonic complex built from partials at 2f_1, 3f_1, 4f_1,\dots is still periodic with period T = 1/f_1 — the greatest common divisor of the partial frequencies is f_1, so the waveform repeats f_1 times a second whether or not the f_1 line is present. The first figure sets up three views of a real C4 piano recording: the waveform repeating on its period T=1/f_1 \approx 3.8 ms, the FFT magnitude as a comb of harmonics, and the cepstrum.
The frequency domain says the same thing in a dual way. The harmonics are equally spaced by f_1, and that spacing is what encodes the pitch. The cepstrum — the spectrum of the log-spectrum (see Chapter 2) — converts a periodic comb of harmonics into a single peak at quefrency 1/f_1. Because deleting a spectral line barely changes the spacing of the rest, this cepstral peak (and the perceived pitch) is robust to removing the fundamental — the reason cepstral pitch estimation works even on telephone speech.
The second figure settles the natural objection with an ideal sawtooth at C5 (f_1 \approx 523 Hz) — synthetic rather than recorded, so the partials sit at exact integer multiples of f_1 with clean 1/n amplitudes and “delete the fundamental” and “shift up an octave” are surgically precise. When we delete f_1, the lowest surviving partial sits at 2f_1 \approx 1046 Hz — exactly the fundamental of C6, one octave up. So why isn’t the fundamental-removed tone simply heard as C6? Because pitch follows the spacing of the harmonics, not the lowest frequency present: the f_1-removed sawtooth still has partials every 523 Hz (1046, 1570, 2093,\dots), whereas a genuine C6 has partials every 1046 Hz (1046, 2093, 3139,\dots). Same lowest frequency, different comb — and the ear tracks the comb. (The tell-tale is the partial at 1570 Hz — the odd multiple 3f_1 — present when f_1 is merely removed but absent one octave up.)



import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy.io.wavfile import read, write as wavwrite

BLUE, RED, GREEN, INK, GREY = '#0d49fb', '#e6091c', '#0a9a4a', '#222222', '#888888'

# ── real C4 recording (figure 1) ────────────────────────────────────────────
def load(name):
    fs, w = read(name)
    x = w[:, 0].astype(float) if w.ndim > 1 else w.astype(float)
    return fs, x / np.max(np.abs(x))
fs, c4 = load('Data/piano_middle_c.wav')
f1 = 261.63                                   # C4 (middle C) fundamental — real recording
f2 = 523.25                                   # C5 — synthetic sawtooth demo (figure 2 + audio)

# ── ideal (band-limited) sawtooth at C5 pitch (figure 2) ────────────────────
dur, N = 2.0, 40
ts = np.arange(int(fs * dur)) / fs
def saw(f0, nmin=1):
    y = np.zeros_like(ts)
    for n in range(nmin, N + 1):
        if n * f0 < 0.45 * fs:
            y += np.sin(2 * np.pi * n * f0 * ts) / n
    return y
saw_full = saw(f2, 1)          # C5: f1, 2f1, 3f1, ...
saw_nof1 = saw(f2, 2)          # fundamental removed: 2f1, 3f1, ...
saw_oct  = saw(2 * f2, 1)      # one octave up (C6): 2f1, 4f1, ...

# ── audio: sawtooth trio (mono int16, normalised, 10 ms fades) ──────────────
def save_wav(name, y):
    y = y / np.max(np.abs(y)); k = int(0.01*fs); r = np.ones_like(y)
    r[:k] = np.linspace(0,1,k); r[-k:] = np.linspace(1,0,k)
    wavwrite(name, fs, (y*r*0.9*32767).astype(np.int16))
save_wav('missing_fundamental_full.wav',   saw_full)
save_wav('missing_fundamental_no_f1.wav',  saw_nof1)
save_wav('missing_fundamental_octave.wav', saw_oct)

# ── analysis helpers (steady segment) ───────────────────────────────────────
i0, L = int(0.3*fs), 16384; win = np.hanning(L)
def spectrum(y):  s = y[i0:i0+L]*win; return np.fft.rfftfreq(L,1/fs), np.abs(np.fft.rfft(s))**2
def magnitude(y): s = y[i0:i0+L]*win; return np.fft.rfftfreq(L,1/fs), np.abs(np.fft.rfft(s))
def cepstrum(y):
    mag = np.abs(np.fft.rfft(y[i0:i0+L]*win)); logX = np.log(mag + 0.01*mag.max())
    c = np.fft.irfft(logX); return np.arange(c.size)/fs, c

# ── FIGURE 1 — real C4 waveform | FFT magnitude | cepstrum ──────────────────
T = 1/f1; t = np.arange(c4.size)/fs
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(11.2, 3.3), layout='constrained')
tw0 = 0.50; twin = (t >= tw0) & (t < tw0 + 0.02)
ax[0].plot((t[twin]-tw0)*1e3, c4[twin], color=INK, lw=1.0)
ax[0].set_title('waveform', fontstyle='italic')
ax[0].set_xlabel('time [ms]'); ax[0].set_ylabel('intensity [arb.]'); ax[0].set_xlim(0, 20)
f, Mg = magnitude(c4); ax[1].plot(f, Mg/Mg.max(), color=INK, lw=0.9)
ax[1].axvline(f1, color=BLUE, ls='--', lw=1.0); ax[1].set_xlim(0,1600); ax[1].set_ylim(0,1.1)
ax[1].set_title('FFT magnitude', fontstyle='italic'); ax[1].set_xlabel('frequency [Hz]')
ax[1].set_ylabel('magnitude [arb.]')
ax[1].text(0.62,0.6,'fundamental\n+ harmonics', transform=ax[1].transAxes, ha='center', fontsize=9)
q, c = cepstrum(c4); m = (q > 1.5e-3) & (q < 0.011)
ax[2].plot(q[m]*1e3, c[m], color=INK, lw=0.9)
ax[2].axvline(T*1e3, color=BLUE, ls='--', lw=1.0); ax[2].set_xlim(1.5,11)
ax[2].set_title('cepstrum', fontstyle='italic'); ax[2].set_xlabel('quefrency [ms]')
ax[2].set_ylabel('amplitude [arb.]'); ax[2].text(T*1e3+0.3, ax[2].get_ylim()[1]*0.8, '$1/f_1$', color=BLUE)
fig.suptitle('Middle C (C4) — waveform, spectrum, cepstrum',
             fontsize=14, fontweight='bold', fontstyle='italic', color=INK)
plt.savefig('figure_missing_fundamental.png', dpi=200, bbox_inches='tight')

# ── FIGURE 2 — sawtooth full | f1 removed | one octave up (each normalised) ─
plt.close('all')
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(11.2, 3.4), layout='constrained')
panels = [('sawtooth $f_1$ (C5)',         saw_full, f2,   BLUE,  'spacing 523 Hz'),
          ('sawtooth — $f_1$ removed',    saw_nof1, f2,   RED,   'spacing 523 Hz'),
          ('sawtooth — one octave up',    saw_oct,  2*f2, GREEN, 'spacing 1046 Hz')]
for j,(label,y,fp,col,sp) in enumerate(panels):
    f, P = spectrum(y); ax[j].plot(f, P/P.max(), color=col, lw=1.0)
    ax[j].axvline(fp, color=GREY, ls='--', lw=0.8)
    ax[j].set_xlim(0,5200); ax[j].set_ylim(0, 1.1)
    ax[j].set_title(label); ax[j].set_xlabel('frequency [Hz]')
    ax[j].text(0.5,0.97,sp, transform=ax[j].transAxes, ha='center', va='top', fontsize=8, color=GREY)
    ax[j].text(0.93,0.86,'♫', transform=ax[j].transAxes, ha='center', fontsize=15, color=col)
ax[0].set_ylabel('power [norm.]')
fig.suptitle('Same lowest frequency, different pitch — sawtooth without $f_1$  vs  a one-octave-up sawtooth',
             fontsize=12.5, fontweight='bold', fontstyle='italic', color=INK)
plt.savefig('figure_missing_fundamental_compare.png', dpi=200, bbox_inches='tight')



A real middle C (C4) in three views — the waveform (period T=1/f_1 \approx 3.8 ms), the FFT magnitude (fundamental + harmonic comb), and the cepstrum (a single rahmonic peak at quefrency 1/f_1):




Real C4 piano note: waveform, FFT magnitude, and cepstrum. The cepstrum turns the harmonic comb into one peak at quefrency 1/f_1 (its slight shift below the dashed line reflects the piano’s mild inharmonicity — see the inharmonicity example).



Now switch to an ideal sawtooth at C5 (f_1 \approx 523 Hz), delete its fundamental, and set the result beside a sawtooth one octave up (C6). Both have their lowest energy at 2f_1 \approx 1046 Hz, but the f_1-removed sawtooth keeps a 523 Hz comb (so it is still heard as C5) while the octave-up sawtooth has a 1046 Hz comb:




Left: complete C5 sawtooth, comb spaced by 523 Hz. Middle: fundamental removed — its lowest partial is now at 2f_1 \approx 1046 Hz, the same as C6, but the harmonics stay spaced by 523 Hz. Right: a sawtooth one octave up (C6), spaced by 1046 Hz. The give-away is the partial at 1570 Hz (3f_1): present when f_1 is merely removed, absent one octave up. Same lowest frequency, different comb — and the ear follows the comb, so the middle panel is still heard as C5.



Listen for yourself — the first two are the same pitch (C5) even though the fundamental is gone from the second; the third is a genuine C6, an octave higher:



sawtooth — C5f_1 \approx 523 Hz


fundamental removedonly \geq 2f_1 · still C5


one octave upgenuine C6 (2f_1 \approx 1046 Hz)




















The fundamental-removed sawtooth sounds thinner but keeps the pitch of C5 — your auditory system reconstructs the fundamental from the spacing of the surviving harmonics, which is why it is not heard as the C6 that shares its lowest frequency. The cepstrum does the same job mathematically: a single rahmonic peak at 1/f_1, robust to a missing spectral line. It is the audible counterpart of the piano-cepstrum example and the Chapter 2 treatment of the cepstrum as a “spectrum of a spectrum”.

See Chapter 2 — Cepstrum for how the log-spectrum turns a harmonic comb into a single quefrency peak, and the Piano String Inharmonicity example for the same tone analysed for stiffness.

Left: complete C5 sawtooth, comb spaced by 523 Hz. Middle: fundamental removed — its lowest partial is now at 2f_1 \approx 1046 Hz, the same as C6, but the harmonics stay spaced by 523 Hz. Right: a sawtooth one octave up (C6), spaced by 1046 Hz. The give-away is the partial at 1570 Hz (3f_1): present when f_1 is merely removed, absent one octave up. sawtooth — C5f_1 \approx 523 Hz


fundamental removedonly \geq 2f_1 · still C5


one octave upgenuine C6 (2f_1 \approx 1046 Hz)




















The fundamental-removed sawtooth sounds thinner but keeps the pitch of C5 — your auditory system reconstructs the fundamental from the spacing of the surviving harmonics, which is why it is not heard as the C6 that shares its lowest frequency. It is the audible counterpart of the piano-cepstrum example and the Chapter 2 treatment of the cepstrum as a “spectrum of a spectrum”.

title: Aliasing & the Nyquist Folding Receiver
text:
A wideband receiver wants to watch many GHz but can only afford a slow ADC. The NYFR deliberately undersamples the whole band so every Nyquist zone folds down onto the first — and drives the sample-and-hold with a phase-modulated clock instead of a uniform one. If the sampling instants carry a small sinusoidal jitter \delta t(k) = A_j \sin(2\pi f_m k / f_s), a tone at RF frequency f_\text{RF} picks up an induced phase

\phi(k) = 2\pi f_\text{RF}\,\delta t(k) = \underbrace{2\pi f_\text{RF} A_j}_{\text{FM index}}\,\sin\!\left(2\pi \tfrac{f_m}{f_s} k\right).

The tone still lands at its baseband alias, but now wearing an induced FM whose depth is proportional to f_\text{RF} — i.e. to the Nyquist zone. Read the FM depth off a spectrogram and you recover which zone the signal came from, and hence its true frequency. One slow ADC, the whole band, ambiguity resolved.

title: Chorus-Wave Polarization (SVD)
text:
← Back to Gallery
Topic: Multi-channel SVD wave analysis — recovering a wave’s propagation direction and polarization from a single spacecraft’s three-component magnetic field. Chapter: 8 — Multi-Channel Analysis



Whistler-mode chorus is one of the most important wave modes in near-Earth space: these rising-tone electromagnetic emissions accelerate radiation-belt electrons to relativistic energies and scatter them into the atmosphere to light up the diffuse aurora. The Japanese Arase (ERG) satellite records the three-component magnetic field \mathbf{B}(t) of these waves with its Waveform Capture (WFC) receiver.
But a single spacecraft is one moving point: it measures a time series, not a spatial pattern, so it cannot directly see the wave vector \mathbf{k}. The trick is to bring in Maxwell’s equations. In Fourier space \nabla\cdot\mathbf{B}=0 becomes \mathbf{k}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{B}}(\omega)=0 — the wave vector must be perpendicular to the magnetic fluctuation. That single parameter-free constraint, applied across a spectrum of measurements, is enough to reconstruct the propagation direction and the full polarization state.



Form the 3\times3 spectral matrix from the three field components,

\hat{S}_{ij}(\omega) = \langle \hat{B}_i(\omega)\,\hat{B}_j^*(\omega)\rangle,

averaged over neighbouring times and frequencies. The wave vector is the direction \boldsymbol{\kappa} that best satisfies \hat{S}\boldsymbol{\kappa}=0. Santolík et al. (2003) stack the real and imaginary parts of \hat S into a 6\times3 matrix A and solve it by singular value decomposition, A = U\,W\,V^{\mathsf T}. The three singular values W_0 \ge W_1 \ge W_2 then read out the wave’s geometry directly:

wave-normal angle — the angle between \boldsymbol{\kappa} (from the smallest singular vector) and the background field \mathbf{B}_0;
planarity F = 1 - \sqrt{W_2/W_0} — whether the fluctuations lie in a single plane (one common \mathbf{k});
ellipticity W_1/W_0 — linear vs circular polarization;
compressibility and degree of polarization — how transverse and how coherent the wave is.




import numpy as np
import bottleneck as bn

# coef: short-time Fourier coefficients of the 3 magnetic components, shape (freq, time, 3)
# --- spectral matrix S_ij = <B_i B_j*>, smoothed over frequency and time ---
spec = np.einsum('fti,ftj->ftij', coef, coef.conj())
spec = bn.move_mean(spec, window=freq_window, min_count=1, axis=0)
spec = bn.move_mean(spec, window=time_window, min_count=1, axis=1)

# --- Santolik 6x3 augmented matrix [Re S ; Im S], then SVD at every (f, t) ---
spec_63 = np.concatenate([spec.real, spec.imag], axis=-2)
u, s, vh = np.linalg.svd(spec_63, full_matrices=False)   # s: three singular values, descending

planarity         = 1 - np.sqrt(s[:, :, 2] / s[:, :, 0])   # 1 = one common wave vector
ellipticity_along_k = s[:, :, 1] / s[:, :, 0]              # 0 = linear, 1 = circular
kappa = vh[:, :, 2, :]                                     # wave-normal direction (smallest sing. vector)
wave_normal_angle = np.degrees(np.arccos(np.abs(kappa @ b0_hat)))   # angle to background field







Whistler-mode chorus observed by Arase/ERG-WFC on 2017-03-31. Top: the three-component magnetic waveform. Below it, the power spectrogram shows discrete rising-tone chorus elements near 1–2 kHz, and the SVD spectral-matrix analysis returns, frequency-by-frequency, the compressibility, ellipticity (along k and along B), wave-normal angle, coherency, planarity, and degree of polarization.



The stack of panels is a complete wave-mode diagnosis of the chorus emissions from a single spacecraft. Wherever the spectrogram lights up with a chorus element, the SVD panels agree on a consistent story: low compressibility (blue — the fluctuations are transverse, not compressional), ellipticity near 1 and a right-handed sense along \mathbf{B} (circular polarization), a small wave-normal angle (blue — the waves propagate nearly along the background field), and high planarity, coherency, and degree of polarization (red — a single, well-defined, highly polarized wave vector). That combination — transverse, right-hand circular, quasi-field-aligned, coherent — is the textbook signature of whistler-mode chorus, read straight off the singular values. One receiver, three components, and Maxwell’s \nabla\cdot\mathbf{B}=0 turn a time series into the full propagation geometry.

See Chapter 8 for the spectral matrix, the McPherron/Means/Santolík estimators, and field-aligned-coordinate polarization.

title: Airy Diffraction — Theory vs. Experiment
text:
← Back to Gallery
Topic: The Hankel transform — the 2-D radial “spectrum” of a circular aperture, validated against a real laser-diffraction photograph. Chapter: 3 — Power Spectral Density



When monochromatic light passes through a circular aperture, the far-field pattern is the 2-D Fourier transform of the aperture — and for a shape with rotational symmetry the 2-D transform collapses to a 1-D Hankel transform (a Fourier transform in the radial coordinate, with a Bessel-function kernel). The zeroth-order Hankel transform of a top-hat disk is the famous Airy pattern: a bright central disk ringed by fading concentric circles. It sets the diffraction limit of every telescope, microscope, and camera lens.
This example takes the Hankel-transform prediction and holds it up against a real photograph of laser light through a pinhole.



Normalising the radial coordinate by the Airy radius r_\text{Airy} = 1.22\,\lambda f/D, the intensity profile is

I(r) = \left[\frac{2 J_1(u)}{u}\right]^2, \qquad u = 1.22\,\pi\, \frac{r}{r_\text{Airy}},

where J_1 is the first-order Bessel function. What theory pins down exactly is the geometry: the dark rings sit at the zeros of J_1, whose radii are in the fixed, parameter-free ratio 1 : 1.83 : 2.66 : 3.48 : \dots — independent of wavelength, aperture size, or distance. If a real diffraction pattern shows rings in that ratio, it is diffraction from a circular aperture, full stop.



import numpy as np
from scipy.special import j1, jn_zeros
from scipy.optimize import minimize
from PIL import Image

def airy(q):                                   # ideal Airy intensity, q = r / r_Airy
    u = 1.22 * np.pi * q
    return np.where(u == 0, 1.0, (2 * j1(u) / u)**2)

zeros_q = jn_zeros(1, 6) / jn_zeros(1, 1)       # dark-ring radii, in units of r_Airy

# --- EXPERIMENT: a real photo of a red laser through a 0.09 mm pinhole ---
srgb_lin = lambda c: np.where(c/255 <= 0.04045, c/255/12.92, ((c/255 + 0.055)/1.055)**2.4)
I = srgb_lin(np.asarray(Image.open('airy_experiment_pinhole.jpg').convert('RGB'))[:, :, 0])
ys, xs = np.indices(I.shape)

# the true centre is the one that makes the rings concentric = minimum azimuthal variance
def azim_var(c):
    r = np.hypot(xs - c[0], ys - c[1]).ravel(); m = r < 1400
    b = (r[m] / 1400 * 180).astype(int); v = I.ravel()[m]
    mean = np.bincount(b, v, 180) / np.maximum(np.bincount(b, None, 180), 1)
    return np.nansum((v - mean[b])**2)
cx, cy = minimize(azim_var, [I.shape[1]/2, I.shape[0]/2], method='Nelder-Mead').x

# azimuthally average into a radial profile, then fit the single scale r_Airy to the dark rings
r = np.hypot(xs - cx, ys - cy)
bins = np.linspace(0, 1500, 751)
prof = np.array([np.median(I[(r >= a) & (r < b)]) for a, b in zip(bins[:-1], bins[1:])])
# dark-ring radii -> least-squares r_Airy against jn_zeros(1, k); compare prof to airy(rc / r_Airy)







The Airy pattern of a circular aperture. (a) the ideal pattern from the Hankel transform, [2J1(u)/u]², with the theoretical J1 zeros dashed; (b) a real red-laser photograph through a 0.09 mm pinhole (65 mm downstream), the same theoretical rings overlaid; (c) the azimuthally-averaged experimental profile tracking the simulated curve, dark rings at the parameter-free ratio 1 : 1.83 : 2.66.



Panel (a) is pure theory — the squared Hankel transform of a disk. Panel (b) is a real photograph (public domain, B. Bautsch) of red laser light through a 0.09 mm pinhole. The only free parameter recovered from the image is the overall scale r_\text{Airy}; everything else is fixed by the transform. The same dashed circles — the scaled zeros of J_1 — drop squarely into the dark gaps of both the simulation and the photograph, and panel (c) shows the measured radial profile following the ideal [2J_1(u)/u]^2 curve to within a few percent, with the first three dark rings landing at 1 : 1.83 : 2.66. The fitted first null, r_\text{Airy}\approx 0.53 mm, matches 1.22\,\lambda f/D for a $$600 nm laser and the quoted pinhole; the central Airy disk encloses 83.8 % of the diffracted energy.
A small but nice piece of signal processing makes the comparison work: to average a real photo azimuthally you must first find the true centre, done here by minimising the azimuthal variance — the centre at which the rings are most perfectly concentric — after undoing the camera’s sRGB gamma so the pixel values are linear in intensity.

See Chapter 3 for the Hankel transform, its relation to the 2-D Fourier transform, and the quasi-discrete (QDHT) implementation.

title: Heat Conduction — Solving PDEs with the FFT
text:
← Back to Gallery
Topic: The pseudo-spectral method — turning a partial differential equation into one decoupled ODE per Fourier mode, and solving it exactly with the FFT. Chapter: 4 — More about FFT Companion: Electromagnetic Waves — Solved with the FFT



Most physical fields — temperature, pressure, the electromagnetic field — obey partial differential equations involving spatial derivatives. In real space a derivative couples every grid point to its neighbours, which is what makes PDEs hard. But a derivative is diagonal in Fourier space: differentiating e^{ikx} just multiplies it by ik. So the Fourier transform turns

\frac{\partial}{\partial x} \;\longrightarrow\; ik, \qquad \nabla^2 \;\longrightarrow\; -k^2,

and a linear, constant-coefficient PDE collapses into a family of independent ordinary differential equations — one for each Fourier mode — that often have a closed-form solution. This is the pseudo-spectral method, and the FFT makes it fast.



Take the 2-D heat equation \partial_t T = \alpha \nabla^2 T. Fourier-transform in space and the coupled PDE becomes, mode by mode,

\frac{d\hat T(\mathbf k,t)}{dt} = -\alpha\,k^2\,\hat T(\mathbf k,t)
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
\hat T(\mathbf k,t) = \hat T(\mathbf k,0)\,e^{-\alpha k^2 t}.

Each mode simply decays exponentially, at a rate set by k^2 — so short-wavelength (high-k) features die fastest, which is exactly why sharp edges blur first and the field relaxes toward smoothness. The whole solver is: FFT the initial condition, multiply by e^{-\alpha k^2 t}, inverse-FFT. Crucially it is exact in time — you can jump straight to any t with no time-stepping — whereas an explicit finite-difference scheme must crawl forward in steps small enough (\Delta t < \Delta x^2/4\alpha) to stay stable.



import numpy as np
from scipy.fft import fft2, ifft2, fftfreq

N, dx, alpha = 128, 1.0, 1.0
dt = dx**2 / (4 * alpha)                          # finite-difference stability limit
k = 2*np.pi*fftfreq(N, d=dx)
KX, KY = np.meshgrid(k, k, indexing='ij')
k2 = KX**2 + KY**2                                # Laplacian -> -k^2

T0 = np.zeros((N, N)); T0[N//4:3*N//4, N//4:3*N//4] = 1.0   # a hot square block
T0hat = fft2(T0)
T_fd = T0.copy()

for i in range(400):
    t = i * dt
    # (1) FINITE DIFFERENCE — explicit 5-point Laplacian, many tiny stable steps
    lap = (np.roll(T_fd, 1, 0) + np.roll(T_fd, -1, 0) +
           np.roll(T_fd, 1, 1) + np.roll(T_fd, -1, 1) - 4*T_fd) / dx**2
    T_fd += alpha * dt * lap
    # (2) SPECTRAL — exact solution at time t, in a single shot, no stability limit
    T_spec = np.real(ifft2(T0hat * np.exp(-alpha * k2 * t)))







The 2-D heat equation solved two ways as a hot square block diffuses. Left: an explicit finite-difference scheme, crawling forward in many small time steps. Right: the Fourier/spectral solution, T̂(k,t) = T̂(k,0)·exp(−αk²t), evaluated directly. Both give the same diffusing field.



The two panels are the same heat equation solved two ways. On the left, the classic finite-difference method: approximate the Laplacian with a 5-point stencil and step forward in time — but each step must be tiny (\Delta t < \Delta x^2/4\alpha) or the scheme goes unstable and blows up, so reaching a given time takes hundreds of steps. On the right, the spectral method: a single line, \hat T(\mathbf k,t)=\hat T(\mathbf k,0)\,e^{-\alpha k^2 t}, jumps straight to any time with no stability limit and no accumulation of step-by-step error, because in Fourier space every mode evolves independently and exactly. The two tracks agree frame-for-frame — which is the point: the spectral method reaches the same answer, faster and exactly.
That is the appeal of spectral methods: a hard, spatially-coupled PDE becomes pointwise multiplication in k-space. The same trick — \nabla \to i\mathbf k — solves Poisson’s equation (divide by -k^2), advection, the wave equation, and, with the nonlinear term handled pseudo-spectrally, even Navier–Stokes. The heat equation is the easiest case because it has a real, decaying exponential per mode; the electromagnetic-wave companion shows what happens when that exponential becomes oscillatory — Maxwell’s curl equations solved the same spectral way.

See Chapter 4 for the finite-difference comparison, Maxwell’s equations in k-space, and stability of time-stepping schemes.

On the left, the classic finite-difference method: approximate the Laplacian with a 5-point stencil and step forward in time — but each step must be tiny (\Delta t < \Delta x^2/4\alpha) or the scheme goes unstable and blows up, so reaching a given time takes hundreds of steps. On the right, the spectral method: a single line, \hat T(\mathbf k,t)=\hat T(\mathbf k,0)\,e^{-\alpha k^2 t}, jumps straight to any time with no stability limit and no accumulation of step-by-step error, because in Fourier space every mode evolves independently and exactly. The two tracks agree frame-for-frame — which is the point: the spectral method reaches the same answer, faster and exactly.
That is the appeal of spectral methods: a hard, spatially-coupled PDE becomes pointwise multiplication in k-space. The same trick — \nabla \to i\mathbf k — solves Poisson’s equation (divide by -k^2), advection, the wave equation, and, with the nonlinear term handled pseudo-spectrally, even Navier–Stokes. The heat equation is the easiest case because it has a real, decaying exponential per mode; the electromagnetic-wave companion shows what happens when that exponential becomes oscillatory — Maxwell’s curl equations solved the same spectral way.

See Chapter 4 for the finite-difference comparison, Maxwell’s equations in k-space, and stability of time-stepping schemes.

title: Solar-Wind Turbulence Spectrum
text:
← Back to Gallery
Topic: The Welch method on a multi-instrument composite — reconstructing the turbulent cascade of the solar wind across six decades of frequency. Chapter: 5 — Noise



The solar wind — the magnetised plasma streaming out of the Sun — is in a state of fully developed turbulence. Magnetometers on spacecraft such as ACE, Cluster, Wind, and Parker Solar Probe measure a magnetic-field power spectrum that spans roughly six decades in frequency and breaks naturally into a sequence of power-law ranges, each governed by different physics. It is one of the cleanest natural examples of a turbulent energy cascade, and its shape is a direct read-out of how energy is injected, transported, and dissipated in a collisionless plasma. The canonical broadband picture is reviewed by Verscharen, Klein & Maruca (2019); this example reproduces their composite trace spectrum.



Two spectral-analysis ideas do the work.
A multi-instrument composite. No single instrument can span six decades — a slow, long survey resolves the lowest frequencies; a fast, short burst resolves the highest. So the spectrum is stitched together: here ACE MFI over 58 days and 51 hours for the lowest frequencies, and Cluster FGM and STAFF-SC over one hour for the highest. Overlapping bands must agree where they meet.
The Welch method. A raw periodogram of a turbulent signal is enormously noisy — its variance does not shrink as you take more data. Welch’s method splits the record into overlapping segments and averages their periodograms, trading a little frequency resolution for a dramatic reduction in scatter. On the plot the faint traces are the raw periodograms; the bold traces are their Welch averages, and only the latter reveal the power laws cleanly.
The three ranges then stand out:

an injection (“1/f”) range at the lowest frequencies, slope \approx f^{-1}, where large-scale energy is fed in;
an inertial range with the Kolmogorov slope f^{-5/3}, where energy cascades scale-by-scale without dissipating;
a dissipation (kinetic) range beyond the ion-scale break, steepening to \approx f^{-2.8}.




import numpy as np, scipy.signal

# --- the canonical model spectrum: -1 -> -5/3 -> -2.8, continuous at the breaks ---
f_tau, f_ion, A1 = 1.5e-4, 0.4, 3.0            # correlation-scale and ion-scale break
def target_psd(f):
    f = np.asarray(f, float).copy(); f[f == 0] = 1e-30
    P = A1 / f
    C1 = A1 * f_tau**(5/3 - 1);  m = f >= f_tau; P[m] = C1 * f[m]**(-5/3)
    C2 = C1 * f_ion**(2.8 - 5/3); m = f >= f_ion; P[m] = C2 * f[m]**(-2.8)
    return P

# --- each "instrument": synthesise a realistic time series over its band, then estimate its PSD ---
def instrument(fs, T, seed):
    N = int(fs * T); freq = np.fft.rfftfreq(N, 1/fs)
    r = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    g = (r.standard_normal(freq.size) + 1j*r.standard_normal(freq.size)) / np.sqrt(2)
    x = np.fft.irfft(g * np.sqrt(target_psd(freq) * fs * N / 2), n=N)
    raw   = scipy.signal.periodogram(x, fs, window='hann')                    # noisy
    welch = scipy.signal.welch(x, fs, window='hann', nperseg=N // 16)         # averaged -> clean
    return raw, welch

ace_hi = instrument(fs=1.0,   T=51*3600, seed=2)     # ACE MFI, 51 h
cluster = instrument(fs=100.0, T=3600,    seed=4)    # Cluster STAFF-SC, 1 h
# ...stitch ACE (58 d, 51 h) and Cluster (FGM, STAFF-SC) over their respective bands







The solar-wind magnetic-field power spectrum across six decades, composited from four instrument/interval bands (ACE MFI over 58 days and 51 hours; Cluster FGM and STAFF-SC over one hour). Faint traces are raw periodograms; bold traces are their Welch averages. Reference lines mark the f⁻¹ injection range, the f⁻⁵ᐟ³ Kolmogorov inertial range, and the f⁻²·⁸ dissipation range.



The four coloured bands tile the frequency axis from 10^{-6} Hz (slow variations over two months) to tens of hertz (sub-second kinetic fluctuations), and where they overlap they agree — a self-consistent composite. The value of the Welch method is visible directly: each band’s faint raw periodogram scatters over orders of magnitude, and only after segment-averaging (the bold traces) do the three power laws emerge cleanly enough to read a slope. The result is the textbook turbulent cascade — injection at f^{-1}, a Kolmogorov f^{-5/3} inertial range, and an f^{-2.8} dissipation range past the ion-scale break — spanning six decades that no single measurement could ever cover.
A note on the data: this is a faithful reproduction of the canonical composite (following the Verscharen review). Rather than re-download the archival ACE and Cluster intervals, each band’s time series is synthesised from the canonical model spectrum and then estimated — which isolates exactly what the gallery is about, the spectral-estimation technique (raw periodogram vs. Welch, and how bands are stitched), on a signal whose true spectrum is known.

See Chapter 5 for coloured-noise generation, the Welch method, and power-law-noise spectra.

title: Electromagnetic Waves — Solved with the FFT
text:
← Back to Gallery
Topic: Pseudo-spectral time-domain solvers for Maxwell’s equations — replacing the curl operator with i\mathbf k\times, and integrating each mode analytically. Chapter: 4 — More about FFT Companion: Heat Conduction — Solving PDEs with the FFT



The heat-equation companion showed the easy face of the pseudo-spectral method: each Fourier mode of a diffusion problem simply decays, \hat T \propto e^{-\alpha k^2 t}. Light is harder — it oscillates rather than decays — but the same idea carries over. In vacuum, Maxwell’s curl equations are

\frac{\partial \mathbf E}{\partial t} = c^2\,\nabla\times\mathbf B, \qquad
\frac{\partial \mathbf B}{\partial t} = -\,\nabla\times\mathbf E .

The obstacle is the curl: a spatial derivative that couples every grid point to its neighbours. But a derivative is diagonal in Fourier space — \nabla \to i\mathbf k — so the curl becomes an ordinary cross product,

\frac{\partial \hat{\mathbf E}}{\partial t} = i\,c^2\,\mathbf k\times\hat{\mathbf B}, \qquad
\frac{\partial \hat{\mathbf B}}{\partial t} = -\,i\,\mathbf k\times\hat{\mathbf E},

one small, decoupled linear system per wavevector \mathbf k. Combining the two gives \partial_t^2\hat{\mathbf E} = -c^2k^2\,\hat{\mathbf E} — a harmonic oscillator at frequency \omega = c\,k, the exact dispersion relation of light.



How you turn spatial derivatives into numbers is the whole story:

FDTD (finite-difference time-domain, the classic Yee scheme) approximates \nabla\times with nearest-neighbour differences. That stencil has the wrong dispersion relation — high-k waves travel at slightly wrong speeds and directions — so a circular pulse develops grid-dispersion ripples and picks up the square grid’s four-fold anisotropy. It is also bound by the CFL limit c\,\Delta t \le \Delta x/\sqrt2.
PSTD (pseudo-spectral time-domain) computes \nabla\times exactly with an FFT (i\mathbf k\times), keeping leapfrog time-stepping. Spatial dispersion vanishes — the ring stays clean and isotropic — and it needs far fewer points per wavelength.
PSATD (pseudo-spectral analytical time-domain) goes further and integrates each mode’s oscillation analytically in time, with \cos(ckt) and \sin(ckt)/k factors. Like e^{-\alpha k^2 t} for heat, this is exact for any step — one shot jumps straight to time t with no dispersion error at all.

The demo below launches a single Gaussian E_z pulse and lets it radiate. The dashed circle marks the true light-cone r = ct; the question is which solver keeps the wavefront on it.



import numpy as np
from scipy.fft import fft2, ifft2, fftfreq

N, dx, c = 128, 1.0, 1.0
kx = 2*np.pi*fftfreq(N, d=dx); ky = 2*np.pi*fftfreq(N, d=dx)
KX, KY = np.meshgrid(kx, ky, indexing='ij')
k = np.sqrt(KX**2 + KY**2); k[0, 0] = 1e-12            # curl -> i*k x  (·)

X, Y = np.ogrid[:N, :N]
Ez0 = np.exp(-((X - N//2)**2 + (Y - N//2)**2) / 2)     # a point flash of light

dt_fdtd = dx / c / np.sqrt(2)                           # CFL stability limit
dt_spec = np.sqrt(2)/np.pi * dx / c                     # spectral: bigger steps allowed

# (1) FDTD — Yee leapfrog, finite-difference curl  ->  numerical grid dispersion
Ez, Hx, Hy = Ez0.copy(), np.zeros((N,N)), np.zeros((N,N))
for _ in range(int(T/dt_fdtd)):
    Hx -= dt_fdtd*(np.roll(Ez,-1,1) - Ez);  Hy += dt_fdtd*(np.roll(Ez,-1,0) - Ez)
    Ez += dt_fdtd*((Hy - np.roll(Hy,1,0)) - (Hx - np.roll(Hx,1,1)))

# (2) PSTD — exact spatial curl via FFT, leapfrog in time  ->  clean, isotropic ring
Ez, Hx, Hy = Ez0.copy(), np.zeros((N,N)), np.zeros((N,N))
for _ in range(int(T/dt_spec)):
    Ezk = fft2(Ez)
    Hx -= dt_spec*np.real(ifft2(1j*KY*Ezk));  Hy += dt_spec*np.real(ifft2(1j*KX*Ezk))
    Ez += dt_spec*np.real(ifft2(1j*KX*fft2(Hy) - 1j*KY*fft2(Hx)))

# (3) PSATD — analytic time integration of each mode  ->  exact for ANY dt, one shot
Ez0k, Hx0k, Hy0k = fft2(Ez0), fft2(np.zeros((N,N))), fft2(np.zeros((N,N)))
def psatd(t):
    C, S = np.cos(c*k*t), np.sin(c*k*t)/k
    return np.real(ifft2(C*Ez0k + 1j*c*S*(KX*Hy0k - KY*Hx0k)))






A point flash of light spreads as an expanding ring; the dashed circle is the exact light-cone r = ct. FDTD (left) develops trailing ripples and a squarish, grid-aligned wavefront — numerical dispersion from the finite-difference curl. PSTD (middle) computes the curl exactly with an FFT, so the ring stays smooth and round. PSATD (right) integrates each Fourier mode’s oscillation analytically in time and lands the wavefront exactly on the light-cone in a single step.
The three panels solve the same Maxwell equations and differ only in how they evaluate the curl and march in time. FDTD’s nearest-neighbour stencil makes high-frequency components crawl at the wrong speed — the ring frays into ripples and inherits the grid’s four-fold symmetry. Replacing the stencil with the exact spectral derivative i\mathbf k\times (PSTD) erases the spatial error; integrating the resulting \omega = ck oscillation analytically (PSATD) erases the time-stepping error too, exactly as e^{-\alpha k^2 t} did for heat. It is the same lesson in a different key: a spatially-coupled PDE becomes independent, exactly-solvable modes in k-space — whether those modes decay (heat) or oscillate (light).
The price is Fourier’s global reach: the FFT mixes information across the whole grid at once, which assumes periodic boundaries and is harder to parallelise on a GPU than a purely local finite-difference update — which is why FDTD, despite its dispersion, remains the workhorse for large-scale electromagnetic simulation.

See Chapter 4 for Maxwell’s equations in k-space, the FDTD/PSTD/PSATD comparison, and the trade-off between spectral accuracy and parallel locality.

title: Fast Multiplication with the FFT
text:
← Back to Gallery
Topic: The convolution theorem as an algorithm — multiplying huge integers and polynomials in \mathcal{O}(n\log n) instead of \mathcal{O}(n^2). Chapter: 4 — More about FFT



Multiplying two numbers is something you learned in grade school: line up the digits, multiply each pair, and add up the columns. For two n-digit numbers that is n^2 single-digit multiplications — \mathcal{O}(n^2). Fine for 1234\times5678; ruinous when the numbers have millions of digits, as they do in cryptography (RSA), computer algebra, and record-breaking computations of \pi.
The key observation is that grade-school multiplication is a convolution. Write each number in a base B as a list of digits — i.e. as the coefficients of a polynomial evaluated at x=B:

1234 = 1\cdot10^3 + 2\cdot10^2 + 3\cdot10^1 + 4 \;\;\leftrightarrow\;\; a(x)=x^3+2x^2+3x+4 .

Then the product’s digit columns are exactly the convolution of the two digit sequences,

c_k = \sum_{i+j=k} a_i\, b_j ,

followed by carrying the overflow between columns. Polynomial multiplication is this convolution with no carry step at all. So “multiply two big numbers” and “multiply two polynomials” are the same problem: convolve their coefficient sequences.



And convolution is precisely what the FFT makes fast. The convolution theorem says convolution in the sample domain is pointwise multiplication in the frequency domain:

a * b \;=\; \mathcal{F}^{-1}\!\big(\hat a \cdot \hat b\big).

So instead of the n^2 pairwise products, transform both sequences (\mathcal{O}(n\log n)), multiply them elementwise (\mathcal{O}(n)), and transform back (\mathcal{O}(n\log n)). The whole multiply drops to \mathcal{O}(n\log n). Add the carry pass and you have the heart of Schönhage–Strassen, the algorithm behind every big-integer library (GMP, Python’s own int for very large values) and the multi-trillion-digit \pi computations.
The worked example below multiplies 1234\times5678 by convolving the digit lists to [5,16,34,60,61,52,32] and then carrying the tens, recovering 7\,006\,652 — and the benchmark shows the FFT route overtaking schoolbook multiplication once the numbers pass a few hundred digits.



import numpy as np

def fft_multiply(a, b, base=10):
    """Multiply two digit lists (least-significant digit first) via the FFT."""
    n = 1 << (len(a) + len(b) - 1).bit_length()      # zero-pad to a power of two
    prod = np.fft.rfft(a, n) * np.fft.rfft(b, n)      # convolution theorem
    c = np.fft.irfft(prod, n).round().astype(np.int64)
    out, carry = [], 0                                # ripple the carries
    for x in c:
        x += carry; out.append(int(x % base)); carry = int(x // base)
    while carry:
        out.append(carry % base); carry //= base
    return out                                        # least-significant digit first

a = [4, 3, 2, 1]      # 1234, little-endian
b = [8, 7, 6, 5]      # 5678
digits = fft_multiply(a, b)                           # -> [2,5,6,6,0,0,7]
value  = int(''.join(map(str, digits[::-1])))         # 7006652
assert value == 1234 * 5678                           # exact, despite floating-point FFTs







Left: multiplying 1234 × 5678 by convolving their digit sequences gives [5, 16, 34, 60, 61, 52, 32]; carrying the tens between columns yields 7,006,652. Right: measured multiply time versus operand size — direct (schoolbook) convolution scales as O(n²) while the FFT-based multiply scales as O(n log n), the two crossing at a few hundred digits.



The left panel is grade-school multiplication laid bare: each stem is one column sum c_k=\sum_{i+j=k}a_ib_j, the linear convolution of the two four-digit sequences. Values above 9 (like 61) are perfectly legal at this stage — the carry pass afterwards ripples the overflow leftward to produce the final decimal digits, 7\,006\,652. Nothing here is approximate: even though the FFT works in floating point, the exact integer answer is recovered by rounding, because the true column sums are modest integers.
The right panel is the payoff. Direct convolution (np.convolve, the schoolbook method) climbs along the \mathcal{O}(n^2) reference slope; the FFT multiply (fftconvolve) follows the far gentler \mathcal{O}(n\log n) slope. For small operands the FFT’s transform overhead makes it slower — schoolbook wins below the crossover near n\approx300 — which is exactly why real libraries switch algorithms by size: schoolbook for small numbers, Karatsuba in the middle, and FFT-based Schönhage–Strassen only for the truly enormous. The same three lines of code that compute a spectrum turn out to be the fastest known way to multiply.

See Chapter 4 for the convolution theorem, the Cooley–Tukey FFT, and Bluestein’s algorithm — itself a multiplication-as-convolution trick that lets the FFT handle prime-length transforms.

title: Fast Multiplication with the FFT
text:
Multiplying two numbers is something you learned in grade school: line up the digits, multiply each pair, and add up the columns. For two n-digit numbers that is n^2 single-digit multiplications — \mathcal{O}(n^2). Fine for 1234\times5678; ruinous when the numbers have millions of digits, as they do in cryptography (RSA), computer algebra, and record-breaking computations of \pi.
The key observation is that grade-school multiplication is a convolution. Write each number in a base B as a list of digits — i.e. as the coefficients of a polynomial evaluated at x=B:

1234 = 1\cdot10^3 + 2\cdot10^2 + 3\cdot10^1 + 4 \;\;\leftrightarrow\;\; a(x)=x^3+2x^2+3x+4 .

Then the product’s digit columns are exactly the convolution of the two digit sequences,

c_k = \sum_{i+j=k} a_i\, b_j ,

followed by carrying the overflow between columns. Polynomial multiplication is this convolution with no carry step at all. So “multiply two big numbers” and “multiply two polynomials” are the same problem: convolve their coefficient sequences.

title: Fast Multiplication with the FFT
text:
And convolution is precisely what the FFT makes fast. The convolution theorem says convolution in the sample domain is pointwise multiplication in the frequency domain:

a * b \;=\; \mathcal{F}^{-1}\!\big(\hat a \cdot \hat b\big).

So instead of the n^2 pairwise products, transform both sequences (\mathcal{O}(n\log n)), multiply them elementwise (\mathcal{O}(n)), and transform back (\mathcal{O}(n\log n)). The whole multiply drops to \mathcal{O}(n\log n). Add the carry pass and you have the heart of Schönhage–Strassen, the algorithm behind every big-integer library (GMP, Python’s own int for very large values) and the multi-trillion-digit \pi computations.
The worked example below multiplies 1234\times5678 by convolving the digit lists to [5,16,34,60,61,52,32] and then carrying the tens, recovering 7\,006\,652 — and the benchmark shows the FFT route overtaking schoolbook multiplication once the numbers pass a few hundred digits.

title: Fast Multiplication with the FFT
text:
import numpy as np

def fft_multiply(a, b, base=10):
    """Multiply two digit lists (least-significant digit first) via the FFT."""
    n = 1 << (len(a) + len(b) - 1).bit_length()      # zero-pad to a power of two
    prod = np.fft.rfft(a, n) * np.fft.rfft(b, n)      # convolution theorem
    c = np.fft.irfft(prod, n).round().astype(np.int64)
    out, carry = [], 0                                # ripple the carries
    for x in c:
        x += carry; out.append(int(x % base)); carry = int(x // base)
    while carry:
        out.append(carry % base); carry //= base
    return out                                        # least-significant digit first

a = [4, 3, 2, 1]      # 1234, little-endian
b = [8, 7, 6, 5]      # 5678
digits = fft_multiply(a, b)                           # -> [2,5,6,6,0,0,7]
value  = int(''.join(map(str, digits[::-1])))         # 7006652
assert value == 1234 * 5678                           # exact, despite floating-point FFTs

text:

title: Filtering Light Pollution from a Starfield
text:
← Back to Gallery
Topic: Filter design in two dimensions — separating a smooth light-pollution gradient from point-like stars by where they live in the spatial-frequency plane. Chapter: 6 — Signal Processing



Anyone who has pointed a camera at the night sky knows the problem: instead of a black background peppered with stars, the frame carries a bright, uneven wash of skyglow — streetlight scattered back down by haze, plus the atmosphere’s own airglow — brightest toward the horizon. It swamps the faint stars and tilts the whole frame.
The data here is a real photograph: Night Sky Over the Maple Trees (Mmfgh, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 4.0), a wide-field exposure over the Vermont Appalachians. Even at this dark site, the horizon glow sweeps a strong brightness gradient across the bottom of the frame — the working example below is a tree-free sky crop, converted to luminance.
The saving grace is that skyglow and stars occupy completely different spatial scales. Light pollution is a smooth gradient — it varies gently across the entire frame, so all of its energy sits at very low spatial frequencies. A star, by contrast, is a near-point source: a sharp spike a couple of pixels wide, which spreads its energy across high spatial frequencies. This is the two-dimensional version of the everyday filtering problem from Chapter 6 — a slow drift riding under a fast signal — and the same tool applies: build a filter that keeps one frequency band and rejects the other.



Take the 2-D FFT of the frame and the two components fall into different places: the skyglow piles up in a tight blob around the origin (\mathbf k \approx 0), while the stars scatter power out to the edges. So the filter design is a high-pass:

Estimate the background by keeping only the low-frequency core — multiply the spectrum by a smooth Gaussian low-pass e^{-k^2/2k_c^2} and transform back. That reconstructs the skyglow alone.
Subtract it. What remains is the high-pass residual: stars on a flat, near-black sky.

Choosing the cutoff k_c is the whole craft, exactly as when picking a 1-D filter’s corner frequency. Too high and you start eating the stars’ wings and any real extended nebulosity; too low and the gradient leaks through. One subtlety carries over from 1-D filtering too: a periodic FFT treats opposite edges as neighbours, so a frame that is brighter on one side than the other has a discontinuity at the wrap-around — left unhandled it rings along the borders. Padding the image with a mirror reflection before transforming removes that seam, the 2-D analogue of windowing.



import numpy as np
from scipy.ndimage import gaussian_filter

from PIL import Image
# real photo: "Night Sky Over the Maple Trees" (Mmfgh, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 4.0)
im = Image.open('Night_Sky_Over_the_Maple_Trees.jpg').convert('L')
polluted = np.asarray(im.crop((1350, 100, 3800, 2550))                # sky-only crop
                        .resize((1024, 1024), Image.LANCZOS), float) / 255.0

kc  = 0.008                                        # cutoff spatial frequency [cycles/pixel]
pad = polluted.shape[0] // 2

# reflect-pad so the periodic FFT sees no brightness jump at the edges (no ringing)
P  = np.pad(polluted, pad, mode='reflect'); M = P.shape[0]
kx = np.fft.fftfreq(M); KX, KY = np.meshgrid(kx, kx)
lowpass = np.exp(-(KX**2 + KY**2) / (2 * kc**2))   # smooth 2-D low-pass = background model

background = np.real(np.fft.ifft2(np.fft.fft2(P) * lowpass))[pad:-pad, pad:-pad]
cleaned    = polluted - background                 # high-pass: skyglow removed, stars kept







Four panels. (a) The real night-sky crop: thousands of stars and the Milky Way band, riding on a glow gradient that brightens toward the horizon at the bottom. (b) Its 2-D spatial-frequency spectrum (Hann-windowed for display) — the glow’s energy is concentrated in the bright low-k core inside the dashed circle, while star energy fills the rest of the plane. (c) The low-pass reconstruction of that core: the smooth skyglow model the filter removes — note it has also absorbed the Milky Way’s large-scale luminosity. (d) The high-pass result — the same stars on a flat, dark sky.



Panel (b) is why this works at all: the glow collapses into the bright core at the centre of the frequency plane, cleanly separated from the star field that fills the rest. The Gaussian low-pass (dashed circle) scoops out just that core to build the skyglow model in panel (c) — a smooth surface tracing the horizon glow, with no stars in it. Subtracting it leaves panel (d): the coarse background brightness swing drops from 0.19 to 0.03 (six-fold flatter), and the star field stands on a uniform dark sky from corner to corner.
The real photo also demonstrates the method’s honest limit better than any synthetic test could. The Milky Way is genuinely extended structure — its cloud-like luminosity lives at the same low spatial frequencies as the glow, so panel (c) shows the background model swallowing it, and in panel (d) the galactic band survives only through its fine-grained star clouds while its diffuse light is dimmed. That is the same trade-off a 1-D high-pass makes when a signal and its baseline drift overlap in frequency, and it is exactly why astrophotographers reach for gentler cutoffs, masked background models (mask the Milky Way before fitting), or wavelet-based tools when they want to keep the nebulosity. Choosing where to cut is the filter design.

See Chapter 6 for FIR/IIR filter design, choosing a filter’s cutoff and order, and the artefacts of over-aggressive filtering.

title: Notching Out 60 Hz Mains Hum
text:
← Back to Gallery
Topic: The notch (band-stop) filter — surgically removing power-line interference from a biomedical signal without touching the rest of the spectrum. Chapter: 6 — Signal Processing



Almost every measurement made near mains electricity picks up a steady hum at the power-line frequency — 60 Hz in the Americas, 50 Hz across most of the rest of the world — plus its harmonics at 120, 180 Hz… It leaks in capacitively through cables and electrodes, and it is the bane of high-gain instruments: an ECG records millivolts from the heart, so a few millivolts of 60 Hz pickup can bury the trace. You can see it below as the fuzzy grey band riding on top of the heartbeat.
The interference is almost the opposite of the light-pollution gradient in the companion example: there the contaminant was spread smoothly in space; here it is razor-sharp in frequency, a single spectral line (and its harmonics) sitting at a precisely known location. That is the ideal target for a notch filter.



A notch (or band-stop) filter is designed to have a gain of essentially zero in an extremely narrow band around one frequency, and a gain of one everywhere else. scipy.signal.iirnotch(f0, Q, fs) builds a second-order IIR notch: the quality factor Q = f_0/\Delta f sets how narrow the notch is — a high Q carves out a sliver just wide enough to swallow the 60 Hz line while leaving the neighbouring ECG frequencies (the QRS complex spreads up to ~40 Hz) untouched.
Two practical points from Chapter 6 matter here:

Mains hum is not a pure sinusoid, so it also appears at harmonics. Cascade a notch at 60, 120, and 180 Hz to catch them all.
An IIR notch has nonlinear phase, which would distort the sharp QRS edges if applied causally. Running it forward and backward with filtfilt cancels the phase entirely (zero-phase filtering), preserving the waveform’s timing — exactly the concern the linear-phase example is about.




import numpy as np
from scipy.signal import iirnotch, filtfilt

fs = 500                                     # ECG sample rate [Hz]
# noisy = clean ECG + 60/120/180 Hz mains hum

clean = noisy.copy()
for f0 in (60, 120, 180):                    # fundamental + harmonics
    b, a = iirnotch(f0, Q=30, fs=fs)         # narrow band-stop, Q = f0/bandwidth
    clean = filtfilt(b, a, clean)            # zero-phase: no waveform distortion







Three panels. (a) An ECG in the time domain: the grey trace carries a thick 60 Hz hum that obscures the P and T waves; the red trace, after notch filtering, shows a clean heartbeat. (b) Power spectra before (grey) and after (red): sharp interference lines at 60, 120 and 180 Hz drop by orders of magnitude while the broadband ECG content below 40 Hz is untouched. (c) The frequency response of a single 60 Hz notch (Q = 30) — a deep, narrow null.



The time trace (a) tells the story at a glance: the raw signal’s heartbeat is smothered under 60 Hz fuzz, and after three cascaded notches the PQRST morphology — the small P wave, the tall R spike, the broad T wave — emerges cleanly. The spectrum (b) shows why it works and why it is safe: the interference is concentrated in three needle-thin lines exactly at the mains harmonics (dotted blue), and the notch response (c) is zero only in a narrow band around each. Everything the cardiologist cares about lives below ~40 Hz, far from the 60 Hz null, so it passes through unchanged.
The trade-off is the same one that governs all filter design: a narrower notch (higher Q) removes less of the surrounding signal but rings longer in time and is more sensitive to the interference drifting off exactly 60 Hz; a wider notch is more forgiving but eats more of the neighbouring spectrum. When the hum wanders — as real mains does — an adaptive notch that tracks the line frequency does better than a fixed one.

See Chapter 6 for IIR filter representations, zero-phase filtfilt filtering, and choosing a filter’s bandwidth and order.

title: AM Demodulation with the Hilbert Transform
text:
← Back to Gallery
Topic: The analytic signal — using the Hilbert transform to pull the slowly-varying envelope out of a fast oscillating carrier. Chapter: 6 — Signal Processing



An amplitude-modulated (AM) signal carries information in its envelope: a high-frequency carrier \cos(2\pi f_c t) whose amplitude is swelled and shrunk by a slow message m(t), giving s(t) = m(t)\cos(2\pi f_c t). This is how AM radio works, but the same shape appears everywhere a slow process modulates a fast oscillation — the beating of two nearby tones, the amplitude of a vibrating machine part, the loudness contour of speech, the pulsing of a laser.
The task of demodulation is to recover m(t) from s(t). You could rectify and low-pass filter (the cheap analog trick), but there is an exact, elegant tool from Chapter 6: the Hilbert transform.



A real signal s(t) has a symmetric spectrum — every cosine is really two counter-rotating phasors, e^{+i\omega t} and e^{-i\omega t}. The Hilbert transform builds the analytic signal s_a(t) = s(t) + i\,\mathcal H\{s\}(t), which keeps only the positive-frequency half. Geometrically it turns the oscillation into a rotating vector, and the length of that vector is exactly the envelope:

s_a(t) = m(t)\,e^{\,i2\pi f_c t}, \qquad |s_a(t)| = m(t).

So the envelope falls straight out as the magnitude of the analytic signal — np.abs(scipy.signal.hilbert(s)) — and, as a bonus, its phase angle gives the instantaneous phase and frequency. No rectifier, no carrier-tracking loop: one transform recovers the message.



import numpy as np
from scipy.signal import hilbert

fs = 4000; t = np.arange(0, 0.5, 1/fs)
msg = 1.0 + 0.6*np.sin(2*np.pi*8*t) + 0.25*np.sin(2*np.pi*19*t + 0.7)   # slow message
am  = msg * np.cos(2*np.pi*400*t)                                        # 400 Hz carrier

analytic = hilbert(am)             # analytic signal (positive-frequency half)
envelope = np.abs(analytic)        # |s_a| = the message, recovered exactly
inst_freq = np.diff(np.unwrap(np.angle(analytic))) / (2*np.pi) * fs      # bonus: freq







Two panels. (a) The AM signal (grey) with its Hilbert envelope (red) laid over the true message (blue dashed); the envelope traces the modulation exactly, top and bottom. (b) The magnitude spectrum: a single carrier line at 400 Hz flanked by symmetric modulation sidebands at ±8 and ±19 Hz — the message frequencies shifted up to the carrier.



Panel (a) is the demodulation working: the red |s_a| curve rides exactly along the peaks of the carrier and coincides with the true message m(t) (blue dashed) to within the noise — a root-mean-square error of a fraction of a percent. What took a tuned analog receiver is three lines of code. Panel (b) explains the structure: modulating a carrier by m(t) shifts the message’s spectrum up to sit around f_c, producing the carrier line at 400 Hz plus a mirror-image pair of sidebands for each message tone (here at 400\pm8 and 400\pm19 Hz). The Hilbert transform’s job is precisely to discard the negative-frequency mirror so that what remains, demodulated back down, is the message alone.
The method’s one requirement is a separation of scales: the envelope must vary slowly compared with the carrier (the spectrum must be narrowband around f_c). When that holds — as it does for AM radio, vibration envelopes, and beat patterns — the analytic-signal envelope is not an approximation but an exact identity.

See Chapter 6 for the Hilbert transform, the analytic signal, and instantaneous amplitude, phase, and frequency.

(b) The magnitude spectrum: a single carrier line at 400 Hz flanked by symmetric modulation sidebands at ±8 and ±19 Hz — the message frequencies shifted up to the carrier.



Panel (a) is the demodulation working: the red |s_a| curve rides exactly along the peaks of the carrier and coincides with the true message m(t) (blue dashed) to within the noise — a root-mean-square error of a fraction of a percent. What took a tuned analog receiver is three lines of code. Panel (b) explains the structure: modulating a carrier by m(t) shifts the message’s spectrum up to sit around f_c, producing the carrier line at 400 Hz plus a mirror-image pair of sidebands for each message tone (here at 400\pm8 and 400\pm19 Hz). The Hilbert transform’s job is precisely to discard the negative-frequency mirror so that what remains, demodulated back down, is the message alone.
The method’s one requirement is a separation of scales: the envelope must vary slowly compared with the carrier (the spectrum must be narrowband around f_c). When that holds — as it does for AM radio, vibration envelopes, and beat patterns — the analytic-signal envelope is not an approximation but an exact identity.

See Chapter 6 for the Hilbert transform, the analytic signal, and instantaneous amplitude, phase, and frequency.

title: Why Linear Phase Matters — FIR vs IIR
text:
← Back to Gallery
Topic: Phase response and group delay — how two filters with the same magnitude response can treat a signal’s shape completely differently. Chapter: 6 — Signal Processing



When we design a filter we usually stare at its magnitude response — how much each frequency is passed or blocked. But a filter does a second thing that is easy to forget: it delays each frequency, by an amount set by its phase response. If different frequencies are delayed by different times, the components of a signal arrive out of step and its shape is mangled — even though every frequency has the “right” amplitude. This is phase distortion, and it is why the choice between an FIR and an IIR filter is not just about efficiency.



The relevant quantity is group delay — the time delay a filter imposes as a function of frequency, \tau(\omega) = -\,d\phi/d\omega.

A symmetric FIR filter has exactly linear phase: its group delay is a constant at all frequencies. Every component is held back by the same number of samples, so the output is the input delayed but otherwise undistorted — the waveform’s shape is preserved perfectly. The cost is efficiency: many taps to get a sharp cutoff.
A causal IIR filter (Butterworth, Chebyshev, …) reaches the same magnitude response with far fewer coefficients, but its phase is nonlinear — group delay varies with frequency, peaking near the cutoff. Different frequencies are delayed by different amounts, so sharp edges smear asymmetrically and overshoot.

The demo passes a square wave — all sharp edges, rich in harmonics — through a 45 Hz low-pass built both ways, and watches what happens to the edges.



import numpy as np
from scipy.signal import butter, firwin, lfilter, group_delay

fs, fc = 1000, 45
x = ((np.arange(0, 1, 1/fs) % 0.2) < 0.1).astype(float)   # 5 Hz square wave

b, a  = butter(6, fc, fs=fs);      y_iir = lfilter(b, a, x)     # IIR: nonlinear phase
taps  = firwin(121, fc, fs=fs);    y_fir = lfilter(taps, 1, x)  # FIR: linear phase

w_i, gd_i = group_delay((b, a), fs=fs)         # IIR group delay varies with frequency
w_f, gd_f = group_delay((taps, 1), fs=fs)      # FIR group delay is flat (constant)







Two panels. (a) A square wave (grey) low-pass filtered two ways: the FIR output (blue, delay-compensated) rings symmetrically around each edge and keeps its shape; the causal IIR Butterworth output (red) has a fast rise but a lagging, asymmetric overshoot that distorts the edges. (b) Group delay versus frequency: the FIR is a flat constant line, while the IIR’s delay rises to a hump near the 45 Hz cutoff and falls off beyond it.



Both filters have essentially the same magnitude response — a 45 Hz low-pass — yet panel (a) shows they treat the square wave very differently. The linear-phase FIR (blue) produces a symmetric result: the Gibbs ringing sits evenly on both sides of each edge, and once you account for its constant delay the pulse shape is faithfully preserved. The causal IIR (red) rises quickly but then overshoots and settles with the ringing trailing after the edge — an asymmetric distortion, because its group delay in panel (b) is not constant: components near the cutoff are held back ~23 samples while high frequencies pass almost immediately, so the edge’s harmonics arrive scrambled in time.
This is the crux of the FIR-versus-IIR decision. When the shape of the waveform carries meaning — an ECG’s QRS complex, a communications pulse, anything you will measure timing or morphology from — linear phase is worth the extra taps. When only the spectral content matters, or when you can afford to filter offline, a cheap IIR run forward-and-backward (filtfilt) cancels its own phase and gives you the best of both: IIR efficiency with zero net phase distortion.

See Chapter 6 for FIR and IIR filter design, phase and group-delay response, and zero-phase filtering.

title: Downsampling Needs an Anti-Alias Filter
text:
← Back to Gallery
Topic: Decimation done right — why you must low-pass before throwing samples away, and what happens when you don’t. Chapter: 6 — Signal Processing



Halving a signal’s sample rate seems like it should be as simple as keeping every other sample. It is not. The aliasing example showed that sampling too slowly makes high frequencies masquerade as low ones; downsampling an already-sampled signal is exactly the same trap sprung a second time. When you keep every M-th sample you drop the effective sample rate by M, which pulls the Nyquist frequency down by M — and anything that was sitting above the new Nyquist folds back into the band as a spurious low-frequency ghost.
The fix, and the reason scipy.signal.decimate exists as a dedicated function, is to filter first: remove everything above the new Nyquist frequency with a low-pass anti-alias filter, and only then discard samples.



Say a 2000 Hz recording contains a wanted 80 Hz tone and an unwanted 700 Hz component, and we want to decimate by M=5 to a 400 Hz rate (new Nyquist = 200 Hz).

Naive (x[::5]): the 700 Hz tone is above 200 Hz, so it aliases. Its apparent frequency folds to |700 \bmod 400| reflected about Nyquist = 100 Hz — a phantom tone that did not exist in the signal and now sits right on top of the band you care about, impossible to remove after the fact.
Proper (decimate): a low-pass anti-alias filter first attenuates everything above 200 Hz — killing the 700 Hz component while it can still be distinguished — and only then keeps every fifth sample. The 80 Hz tone survives; the 700 Hz tone is gone cleanly, with no ghost.

The lesson is the order of operations: band-limit, then subsample. Once the samples are taken, aliasing is irreversible.



import numpy as np
from scipy.signal import decimate

fs = 2000; t = np.arange(0, 3, 1/fs)
x = np.sin(2*np.pi*80*t) + 0.85*np.sin(2*np.pi*700*t)   # keep 80 Hz; 700 Hz is too high

M = 5                                # new rate 400 Hz -> new Nyquist 200 Hz
x_naive = x[::M]                     # WRONG: 700 Hz folds to 100 Hz
x_dec   = decimate(x, M, ftype='fir')   # RIGHT: anti-alias low-pass, then subsample







Three magnitude spectra. (a) The original 2000 Hz signal: a wanted line at 80 Hz and an unwanted one at 700 Hz. (b) After naive downsampling by 5: the 80 Hz line remains but a spurious line appears at 100 Hz — the 700 Hz component folded back below the new 200 Hz Nyquist. (c) After proper anti-aliased decimation: only the 80 Hz line survives; the 700 Hz component has been removed with no ghost.



The three spectra make the failure and the fix unmistakable. In (a) the two tones are cleanly separated at 80 and 700 Hz. Naive decimation (b) keeps the 80 Hz tone but, because 700 Hz now lies beyond the new 200 Hz Nyquist, folds it down to a 100 Hz alias — a tone that was never in the signal, landing squarely in the passband where nothing can distinguish it from real data. Anti-aliased decimation (c) applies the low-pass first, so the 700 Hz energy is gone before subsampling and only the genuine 80 Hz tone remains.
This is why every resampling routine — audio sample-rate conversion, image downscaling, sensor decimation — bundles an anti-alias filter, and why x[::M] is almost never the right way to reduce a sample rate. It is the same theorem as the aliasing example, now framed as a rule for processing: you cannot un-fold an alias, so you must filter before you fold.

See Chapter 6 for decimation, interpolation, and multirate signal processing, and Chapter 1 for the sampling theorem behind aliasing.
